On the Orders of the Day:

I wish to make inquiry of the government concerning the unemployment situation in the city of Winnipeg. I am in receipt, as I believe also are the other representatives of Winnipeg constituencies, of a communication from the mayor of Winnipeg enclosing a letter written by him on the 15th of February to the hon. Minister of Labour (Mr. Murdock), together with a copy of a resolution passed by the city council. It purports to state that an order in council- No. 220-was passed by the government, in which the government undertook, under an arrangement made last year at the Unemployment conference, to make provision for one-third of the relief that would be granted to the city under certain circumstances and after investigation. This order in council,
I believe, dealt only with the case of ex-service men. The resolution in question, which I understand was sent to the Minister of Labour showed, that in Winnipeg at the present time the unemployment relief office is looking after 6,181 unemployed, which would mean that 1,500 would be taken care of under the assistance granted by the government. I am instructed to make inquiry of the government what attitude they purpose taking in connection with this demand for further assistance from the city of Winnipeg.

Mr. Speaker, during the month of December representations came from the Prime Ministers of Manitoba and British Columbia, to ascertain what the purpose of the federal government was to be this winter relative to the conditions ol unemployment that were alleged to exist-After very careful consideration of the unemployment problem as it seemed to exist generally in Canada, it was determined by the government that it would be unnecessary-to adopt any general unemployment relief scheme such as had been in effect during the two preceding winters, and on December 22, a telegram was sent to the Prime Ministers' of Manitoba and British Columbia indicating the view of this government on the subject. From that telegram the following, which evidences the position of the government, is taken:
Information reaching the federal government does not lead to the view that any situation exists at the present time which is at all comparable to that prevailing during the two last preceding winters.
Winnipeg Unemployment

The situation, therefore, as it appears to the federal authorities, is not one which justifies action on their part in assuming at present any portion of the obligations falling customarily to the municipal and provincial authorities.
That information was conveyed to the mayors of a number of cities east and west that had also inquired what the attitude of the federal government was to be during the present winter. During the past thirty days, certain deputations waited upon the government, and representations were made indicating that in certain municipalities in Canada there was a condition of unemployment particularly affecting returned men, that the municipal and provincial authorities had taken no action to alleviate, the result being that in those municipalities relief bodies had been formed composed of returned soldier organizations, charitable organizations, and other welfare societies, with, in some cases, representatives from the municipal authorities on these bodies. It was believed that in such cases it might be advisable for the federal government to assist such organizations formed in that way. The result was that Order in Council No. 220 was passed on the recommendation of the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment. This order provides that in the case of unemployed ex-service men requiring relief, and not being in a position to secure proper assistance from municipal or provincial authorities but obtaining aid only from the organizations to which I have just referred, the federal government would participate to the extent of paying one-third of the disbursements incurred since January 1, 1923. That, in brief, is the position that has been taken up to the present time, and there does not appear to be any necessity whatever for changing the general policy as applicable to the entire Dominion. I am not clear at the moment whether Winnipeg, under Order in Council No. 220, will be able to participate in any way whatsoever, or to secure any assistance from the federal government.
What is the date of that order in council?
The order is dated 5th February.

Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance) moved that the House go into committee on the following proposed resolution.
Resolved, that it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide that a certain convention of commerce dated the fifteenth day of December, in the year one thousand

France-Canada Convention
nine hundred and twenty-two, entered into at Paris by Plenipotentiaries appointed by His Majesty and by the President of the French Republic be approved, and to give effect to the provisions of the said convention.
Motion agreed to and the House went into committee, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The best customer for the surplus products of Canada is the Mother Country, and I have no doubt it will continue to be so. Next to the Mother Country in the volume of our trade is the great republic to the south of us. I have no doubt that, even in the face of the adverse tariff conditions existing to-day, we shall still do a large volume of trade with that country. In comparison with the large figures of the United States and Great Britain our trade with other countries is not great, and I confess that in the present state of European affairs I do not look for any large development of our trade with any European country. Nevertheless, it will be felt, I am sure, by the House, that we should have a watchful eye upon the trade condiLons' of these countries, and make an effort to obtain the best available terms for the products of Canada, even though the trade to be anticipated may not be very large. In the earlier years of our Dominion our trade with France, as well as the trade with other countries, was carried on under the operation of old British treaties. Some of those treaties are still in operation. Thirty years ago it was deemed desirable that we should have a special arrangement with France. Indeed it is an interesting fact that the only foreign country with which up to the present time we have made a commercial treaty is France. We are now making a treaty with Italy, but up to the present time our only trade treaty with a foreign country is with France. Our first treaty was made in 1893. In every treaty that has been made with France, the British ambassador at Paris has been associated with the Canadian representatives. I am safe in saying that the British ambassador has always recognized the fact that the business was Canadian and has left the negotiation of the treaty to a Canadian representative. I have no doubt that was the case in the early treaty with which I had no connection, in the days of Lord Dufferin. But I can testify that has been the case in the years in which I have had some knowledge of such transactions. In the treaty with which I had something to do, as far back as 1907 and 1908, we had the association of the British ambassador of that day, Sir Francis Bertie, afterwwards Lord Bertie, now dead. In the recent negotiations we had the pleasure of being associated with the British Ambassador
at Paris, Lord Hardinge of Penshurst. I want to testify that in the case of both these negotiations the Canadian representative at all times received from the ambassadors the most cordial sympathy and co-operation. The first treaty was signed in 1893 by Sir Charles Tup-per. I am not mentioning the British ambassador, because he was associated in each case. In 1907 a treaty was negotiated by the present Mr. Justice Brodeur and myself. In 1908 a supplementary treaty was' negotiated by myself, to make good a defect that had been found in the earlier treaty. In 1921 a treaty was signed by Sir George Foster as Minister of Trade and Commerce. In the treaty which I now present to the House the signers were my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe) and myself. I again say that in all the negotiations the British ambassador was associated with the Canadian representative, and in all cases the British ambassador gave his cordial co-operation. The negotiation was conducted and controlled entirely by Canada's representatives.
The two treaties of 1907 and 1908 remained in force for a number of years and a considerable volume of trade was developed under them. On 10th September, 1918, France gave a general notice to terminate her commercial treaties. In that case I am sure there was no particular intention to legislate against Canada or against any other country. It was the aim of the French government to have freedom of negotiation in regard to commercial affairs, in view of the new situations that were arising. Notice was given to Canada in consequence of that general determination of the French government. Later the French government agreed to continue the treaty for a further time, changing the period of notice required for its termination. In the treaties previously existing, which they were proposing to terminate, the condition was that they should be terminable on a year's notice. The French government agreed to continue them for a short time, on the condition that they should be subject to a three months' notice. This arrangement was confirmed by an act of the parliament of Canada in 1919. Subsequently, in 1920, the Canadian government gave notice to terminate the treaty. I find that the order in council of that day was passed on the recommendation of the then Acting Minister for External Affairs, Hon. Mr. Rowell. The records do not show any particular reason for giving this notice to terminate the treaty. The notice had been previously given by France. Then France had suspended this notice and agreed to continue the treaty for a while. In
France-Canada Convention

the end the Canadian government, for reasons which I have no doubt were satisfactory, but which are not set forth in the order in council, decided to give notice. The notice to which I refer was given in 1920. Then, in 1921, a new convention was signed by Sir George Foster and was confirmed by legislation a little later. In that new convention provision was made that a number of things for which we had had the minimum tariff before were no longer to take the minimum tariff, but a system of percentages of reduction was introduced. It was also provided in that treaty that it could be terminated at any time on four months' notice. A reading of the treaty plainly shows that it was regarded as only a temporary arrangement, and the expectation was that at an early date Canada would enter into a negotiation for a more comprehensive treaty. The French government applied in the year 1921, through their consul in Montreal, for a negotiation on that subject. It was at a time when the late government was no doubt busy with other things; at all events it was not found convenient to take up negotiations at that time. That was the situation when the present government came into power. The French Consul General at Montreal came to see us shortly after that, and we had some preliminary negotiation and it was then agreed that the matter should be further considered by a conference at Paris. It was under these circumstances that my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries and myself went over to Paris during the recent summer. The treaty which appears before the House contains a number of schedules. The first schedules A. B. and C. touch the question of what France offers Canada. Schedule C. refers to what shall take place in the case of the island of St. Pierre; and then the later schedules D. E. and F. touch what Canada shall give to France.
It would be very desirable if we could get an exchange of minimum tariffs; but for reasons which were strong in the minds of the French government, that could not be accomplished. We shall find in schedule D that France is to receive a fixed rate on a number of articles, those rates being in most cases a little below the Canadian intermediate tariff. On some items where the preferential and the intermediate rates were the same, there is a reduction of duty which will apply, of course, both to the preferential and to the intermediate. This does not, however, affect British manufacturers seriously, because as regards the items referred to the British do not seriously compete. The principal item on which 
we give them a fixed rate of duty is wine. On wines of a lower strength we give them the same rates as were in the old treaty of 1907-OS; but on the stronger wines, on which they received reduced rates in 1907-08, we do not give them any reduction. The rates of duty on that class of wine have since been made higher, and on the stronger wines we do not give anything below the present rate.

I think, if my
hon. friend will allow me, there is a reduction of 10 per cent on the heavier wines. They are included in schedule E as getting a reduction of 10 per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Our rate of duty is 55
cents per gallon, and we do not reduce it. My hon. friend will, I think, find that is correct; but on wines of lower strength they get the same rates as were in the old treaty.
Schedule E comprises quite a long list of French products on which a reduction is made in the form of a discount of 10 per cent on the amount of duty under the intermediate tariff. That is not to be construed as a reduction of 10 per cent in the rate of duty; it is 10 per cent on the amount of the duty. For example, if the duty is 830, and the customer has to pay to the custom house $30, he will receive a discount of 10 per cent, which practically reduces the rate of duty to $27, instead of $30. I might give other examples of that, but that is unnecessary. In schedule F we have three tariff items, touching chiefly woollen clothing and fabrics. While the items are not numerous, they are rather comprehensive in their character, including a large volume of imports. On those three items, it is proposed to apply the same principle, but to increase the rate of discount from 10 to 15 per cent. This would work out in this way. If a duty under the intermediate tariff is 30 per cent, or $30 on $100, a reduction of 15 per cent on the $30 is made. The duty to be paid is thus reduced from $30 to $25.50. Where not otherwise specified, French products are to receive the benefit of the intermediate tariff. Provision is made that in schedules E and F the proportionate difference between the intermediate and general tariffs shall be maintained. The provisions of the old agreement for the encouragement of direct trade are substantially renewed. Then, there are other provisions such as are usually found in commercial treaties, provision under which the parties mutually guarantee to one another equitable conditions.
The loss of revenue in this matter is worthy of consideration. We have to remember that

France-Canada Convention
whatever conditions we grant to France, we shall also grant to a number of nations which enjoy what is called the "favoured nation" principle. On a rough estimate, taking into consideration the business on the basis of last year's operations, our trade with France and with the nations affected by the "favoured nation " arrangement, I estimate that there will be a reduction of duties under the treaty amounting to about $850,000. The favoured nations which are included in this, that is to say the nations which are entitled to what is called the most favoured nation treatment, are Argentina, Colombia, Denmark, Japan, Norway, Sweden, Switzerland and Venezuela. Whatever we grant to France under this arrangement must, of course, be granted to those countries, and I have included the trade from those countries in my estimate of the reduction of taxation.

I take it that
my hon. friend's treaty with Italy will add to the "favoured nation" clause.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I will say that we have
in this estimate included Italy, Italy is not at present a favoured nation, but Italy will come in, and the trade with Italy is included in this rough estimate.
Let us turn to what, in the minds of many, is a more important question, as to what are the terms on which our products are to be taken into France. As I have said, it would be convenient in many ways if we could have simply the French minimum tariff; but the French government will not grant the whole French minimum tariff, nor the "favoured nation" principle generally, to anybody. They treat these things as instruments for negotiation. The French minimum tariff is a moderate tariff; the French general tariff is much higher. By a system of what is called coefficients, the French multiplied the rates of tariff, and the result is that the general tariff is very high. Practically speaking, if the general tariff had to be applied to us, I am afraid it would in most lines of trade be prohibitive. If then, we cannot get the whole minimum tariff of France-and that is the declared policy of France in dealing with all nations- our object must be to get as large a list of items under the minimum tariff as we can. Another point we ought to have in view is that our great competitor in the French market will be our friends to the south, the United States. They are producing many of the same things that we are producing, and if we are to meet competition in the markets of Europe, we must consider the position of the United States. They have at this moment
some advantage over us and I shall have occasion to refer to that later. But one of the strong points that we had to keep in mind was to see that whatever might be the rates of duties levied against our products, we should take pains to get at least as good terms as those given to our chief competitor, the United States. That is a strong feature of our aim, and I am glad to say that in that respect we have fully accomplished our purpose.
We have a large list of items which are given under the minimum tariff, and it will be found that these include most of our important products. In addition to getting the minimum tariff, we get what is very important, a guarantee that as respects all the articles in that list, we shall receive what is called the "most favoured nation" treatment; that is, France will not grant to any country better terms than she grants to Canada as respects articles named in that list.
Then we have another long schedule of goods which are not admitted to the minimum tariff, but which are made the subject of special rates of reduction. The list is somewhat long. .Both that list and the minimum tariff list contain a number of items which, perhaps, on first reading, hon. gentlemen might think were of no importance; but it is well to remember that Canada's industries are developing and that we are producing to-day some things which we did not produce a few years ago. There is every reason to expect that with the development of our trade and our industrial life we shall be able to produce some things which we shall want to export in the future to a larger degree than we have done in the past. That is why many items are included in these schedules which on the first reading may possibly be regarded as not of great importance. On the minimum list we get the best that is going to-day, and we get a guarantee that as respects the wide world no country shall obtain better terms in connection with any one of the items mentioned in the list. That, we think, is an important point. When you come to the next schedule, which is not the minimum tariff, but where you get a certain percentage of reduction, we receive, we are pleased to know, an assurance that in regard to that long list we shall obtain the best terms that are enjoyed by our neighbour, the United States. So that as regards neither the first nor the second list have we any reason to fear the competition of our brethren to the south of us. There is a friendly rivalry between us and we have taken pains to see that we have been given a guarantee that whatever the rates may be, we shall fare as well as the neighbouring republic. In
France-Canada Convention

that respect we can claim we served the purposes we had in view.

Is the minister not sweeping in his statement as to Schedule A? Is France not free to grant lower tariffs than she grants to us, not only to her protectorates *-which, of course, we cannot object to- but also to enemy and adjacent countries?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Perhaps my right hon. friend has been reading Article II.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That article reads:
The grant of the minimum tariff for the products enumerated in schedule A means the treatment of the most favoured 'nation as respects such products, but does not entitle Canada to claim the benefit of any preferential advantage which France may grant to her Protectorates or the benefit of any tariff resulting from economic agreements which France may enter into with border states, or the benefits of any tariff which France may grant for products the importation of which is designed to facilitate financial settlements with those countries that were at war with France during the years 1914-1918.
The first part of that artjcle is a simple assurance, which we readily accept, that we are not to ask the benefit of any preference which France grants her colonies. And we do not permit her to receive the benefit of any preference we see fit to grant any part of the British Empire. The second part of the article, to which my right hon. friend presumably refers, has reference not to the ordinary trade and commerce of the country, but to a peculiar condition that exists to-day in Europe. France is expecting reparations and is taking strong means in her endeavour to obtain them. She may have to make arrangements with Germany by which she will receive German products for the rehabilitating of the devastated regions of her country. That is outside the ordinary channels of trade and commerce, and we thought the request of the French government in that respect was not an unreasonable one. Nor do I think that there is any likelihood of any serious competition arising under that clause. At all events, that is the explanation. Since France expects to receive from Germany many things which do not come within the ordinary scope of trade and commerce but are intended for use in rebuilding the devastated regions, the French government considered that they should not be treated as a matter of ordinary trade, and we were of the opinion that that position was not unreasonable.
What is the significance of the reservation as to border states? What states would that include?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is in almost all treaties some provision for a small area on the border line which is not brought under the operation of the customs. My right hon. friend will find something of the kind in the last treaty. There is a zone on each side of the line in which there is practically free trade between the two countries concerned, and my hon. friend will find a provision of the kind, I am sure, in the last treaty.

With all deference to my hon. friend, who I am sure knows more about it than I do, I hardly think that that could be the significance of this reservation. This article reserves the right to France to enter into treaties with border states, such as Switzerland, Spain, Italy, and Belgium.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think my hon. friend will find that a similar provision is incorporated in most commercial treaties. The explanation is as I have stated, and I know that we had some such arrangement in the last treaty. However, I shall have to look further into that point. Next, we have a provision that if at any time France may grant to the United States larger percentages than are accorded Canada-it is provided that they must give ns the same treatment to-day -then Canada's percentages shall have to be increased to the same extent. These, I think, cover most of the provisions of the treaty.
How do the United States get their preferential treatment to-day?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The United States some years ago were lucky enough to make some arrangement with France whereby the provisions of the tariff of 1910 were to be continued, and the United States were to enjoy certain rates. That condition remains today, but I have my doubts whether it will continue very long. At all events, it is a fact to-day that the United States enjoy advantages which other countries do not, advantages which we in Canada have reason to regret have been granted.
But how did they obtain those advantages-by legislation of their own?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
By treaty and negotiation .with the French government. They were able to stipulate that while other countries would have to pay increased tariffs the United States would not. However, my impression is that that is a condition of affairs which is not likely to last.

France-Caiuida C onvention
How would it be abrogated?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The arrangement could
only cease by the French government giving notice of its termination. That is not a matter within our control. But so long as that arrangement exists we shall get the benefit which so far we have been deprived of. I think it might be well for me to read a few items giving the rates which apply to the United States and to Canada to-day.

Before the minister does so, would he say whether or not it is correct that the United States enjoy these rates without having given any concession, and that they do not to-day give any concession to France in their tariff?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not think they
give any concession, but our main point is that they do get these rates and we do not. My recollection is that they do not give any concession, and I think the arrangement is so unsatisfactory to the French government that in all probability it will not long continue. But so long as it does continue, the inequality and discrimination which have existed in the past as against us will no longer obtain. Here are h few items by way of illustration. On tissues of pure cotton, plain, twilled and drills, per 100 kilogrammes, the rate to-day which Canada pays is 1,364 francs, while the United States enjoys a rate of 440 francs. We shall obtain that rate when this treaty goes into force. On general machinery Canada to-day pays 128 francs and the United States 48. Under the new treaty we shall get the lower rate. On detached parts of machines, etc., the Canadian rate is 344 francs, while the rate which the United States receives, and which we shall obtain after the treaty goes into force, is 107.50 francs. On component parts of copper, pure or alloyed, moulded, wrought, etc., Canada to-day pays 360 francs and the United States 90. We shall hereafter pay that lower rate. Another item on which Canada to-day pays 504 francs under the treaty will be subject to the reduced rate of 126 francs, which is the American rate.
Is any preference given the United States to-day by France on the importation of a Canadian product like nickel?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not tell my hon. friend offhand how nickel is affected. The articles I have mentioned are clearly those in which there is discrimination. I shall be glad to go into the nickel question and let my hon. friend know later.
I think my hon. friend has covered nickel in this treaty.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes. On component parts of machines and shafting, not specified, of two or more metals, etc., we are paying now a rate of 350 francs, the American rate is 140 francs, and we will get the benefit of this reduced rate. On another item of the same class we are paying a rate of 306.25 francs, against the American rate of 122.50, and we will get this lower rate. On another item we are paying at the rate of 262.50 against the American rate of 105, which rate we shall of course get the benefit of. On another item we are paying 175 francs, and we shall get the benefit of the American rate of 70 francs.
On screws, eyebolts, strap hinges, etc., we are paying 784 francs, against the American rate of 294 francs, which reduction we shall get the benefit of. On another item in the same class we are paying 616 francs, while the American rate is 252 francs; we will get the American rate. On another item of the same class we are paying 476 francs, and we shall get the benefit of the American rate of 189 francs. On another item of the same class we are paying 392 francs and shall get the benefit of the reduction to the American rate of 147 francs. On another item of the same class we are payring 1064 francs, and will get the benefit of the American rate of 399 francs.-On another item of the same class where we are now paying 840 francs we will pay the reduced American rate of 315 francs. On another item of the same class on which we are paying 616 francs we will get the reduced rate of 231 francs. On still another item of the same class on which we are paying 560 francs we shall get the benefit of the American rate of 210 francs.
On all these things which I am enumerating the Americans have the advantage to-day, and in some cases that advantage to them and disadvantage to us seriously affects our manufacturing interests.
On household wares and all articles of iron, steel, etc.,-quite a large list-Canada is paying 184.45 francs, the American rate is 59.50 francs. We will get the benefit of that rate. In another case in the same list we are paying 195.30 against the American rate of 63 francs, which of course we get the benefit of. On another item of the same group our rate is 217 francs against the American rate of 70 francs, and we get the advantage of this reduction too. On porcelain we are paying 76 francs, while the Americans are paying 23.75 francs. We will have that reduced rate. On another item in the same

France-Canada Convention
class we are paying 256 francs while the Americans pay only 80 francs. We will get the benefit of that reduced rate. On another item in the same class we are paying 192 francs and will get the benefit of the reduced American rate of 57.60 francs. On still another item we are paying to-day 320 francs against the American rate of 96 francs-* another reduction we will get the benefit of.
Upon skins and hides prepared, varnished, we are paying to-day 2500 francs and we shall get the benefit of the American rate of 625 francs.
On other kinds of nails we are paying to-day 196 francs while the American rate is 66-50. We will get the benefit of this rate.
All the above-mentioned goods originating in and coming from Canada will
4 p.m. enjoy the same tariff rates as like goods the produce of the United States. I think hon. gentlemen will admit that in that respect the treaty removes a very great disadvantage.
I do not wish to magnify the importance of the treaty. As I have already said, the volume of trade we have with France is not very extensive, but whatever it is, it has been the policy of this country for the past thirty years to make special efforts for better trade relations with France, and in that spirit we have approached the negotiations. Of course, it takes two to make a bargain, and more than once in the course of the negotiations we doubted if we would succeed. However, the French government, although looking out for number one, met us in a good spirit. While each side would no doubt like to have something better, I think that we are able to state to parliament that on the whole the arrangement is a fair and reasonable one, and in so far as any treaty can do will help to promote trade between France and Canada.

The minister recited quite a number of items without giving their names and compared the old duty with the new, that is, the American duty that we get to-day with the duty we have been paying heretofore. Will he say that in respect of all these items Canada actually produces them for export?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We are advised by the manufacturers' representatives that all the items I have read are of importance to their interests. As I have already said, in looking over the list you will see many articles which to-day are not important in our export trade. But the development of our manufacturing interests is going on very rapidly to-day, and many of these items which hon. gentlemen may think of little or no importance to-day

have been included in the treaty at the special wish of the manufacturing interests of Canada. They felt that in view of that rapid development it is wise to make provision for the best terms available in order that we may reap the advantage when we do begin to export those items.
Presuming the French government will withdraw these concessions from the United States, do our concessions likewise terminate at that time, or do we revert to our present tariff?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have no authority to say that the French government will withdraw these concessions from the United States, but I can imagine it might be possible. If my hon. friend will read Article 5 he will find it is in these words:
All products originating in and coming from Canada other than those mentioned in schedules A and B to this convention shall be subject in France to the rates of the general tariff of 1910 as long as by virtue of the French decree of March 28th, 1921, such tariff shall continue to be applicable to the products of the United States of America other than those specified in schedule A and schedule B to the French law of March 29th 1910.
If the United States of America should at any time cease to enjoy the benefit of the French decree of March 28th,	1921, products of Canada other than those
enumerated in schedules A and B to this convention shall enjoy a reduction of twenty-five per cent on the difference between the French g nsral tariff and minimum tariff, whatever the rates of these tariffs may be.
So long as France continues the arrange ment we get the same rates. If the rates art withdrawn that will be a matter then foi negotiation between the United States and France, but in any case we get the reduction specified in Article 5.

In Schedule D under the heading of wines, I notice that the rate of duty is 15 cents a gallon for wines of certain alcoholic strength. I would point out to the minister that wines of that strength manufactured in my constituency bear an excise of 30 cents a gallon, so that the wine manufacturers and grape growers are at an absolute disadvantage of 15 cents a gallon as against the imported article laid down in Montreal or any other part of Canada. Is it the minister's intention to do away with the excise, or is our native industry to be left at this big disadvantage?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That raises quite a different question, I can say to my hon. friend. This rate is established under our agreement with the French government, but what rate we shall otherwise establish for any article affected by. this treaty is entirely an open matter for the government and parliament.

France-Canada Convention
I am not unmindful of the point raised by my hon. friend, but that would have to be dealt with by a separate act. It could not come into the treaty itself.

I naturally understand that the two things will go together. It is a very important matter. While in a general way I am in favour of this treaty, because certainly some of the things that the minister has accomplished have taken away some of the disadvantages that other people are under, at the same time it seems to me very unreasonable to place a district such as that where I come from under such a disadvantage. For the minister's information I may say that since the grape growers became aware of this treaty they had a meeting in the county of Lincoln only recently, and the president of their organization advised the farmers of the county of Lincoln not to plant any more vineyards. The despatch says:
At the annual meeting of the shareholders of the Niagara District Grape Growers, Limited, President Welstead in his address referred to the proposed treaty with France under which French wines will be admitted to Canada at fifteen cents per gallon duty, at which rate wines from that country can be unloaded at Montreal cheaper than wine can be manufactured in Ontario. The president also stressed the importance of not adding to new vineyards as there is now sufficient acreage grown to care for the demand.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can only suggest to my hon. friend that he might accept the philosophy that is commonly ascribed to a former prime minister of Great Britain- wait and see. This treaty deals with an agreement with the French government. I might remind my hon. friend that any changes we make in our ordinary Canadian tariff would come most properly at the time of the budget, and before this treaty can be ratified and confirmed the budget will be down. I hope my hon. friend will reserve his conclusion until he hears that.

I just wished to point out this matter to the committee. I am not finding fault without good reason. I am quite aware, as the minister has told us on other occasions, that you cannot make an omelette without breaking eggs, but I do not want the farmers of my county to have all their eggs broken.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the people who have been advising against the growing of grapes must have been intending to encourage the prohibition movement.

I am afraid I shall have to make a few general remarks on the subject of this treaty and to take, somewhat sharply, issue with my hon. friend on ' some of the matters he has covered. In the first place I entirely agree with him in the general sentiment that he expresses as to the advisability of maintaining the closest commercial relationship with France; I think that is something on which we are all agreed. As he pointed out, this action, which was taken in the first instance by a Conservative administration, has been followed by every administration since. We want to deal with France.
I also agree with my hon. friend in what he says as to the unfortunate position of Canada, and agree entirely with what he says as to the unfairness of that position. Why, in some items as a result of the concessions given by France to the United States, the duties are such that it is quite impossible for Canada to compete at all with the United States. My hon. friend went on to say that a great deal might be said as to the unfairness of that, and I entirely agree with him. Our position was that that treatment was entirely unfair, but I am quite sure also that it was not a matter of fixed and definite policy on the part of France. It was something that was done in the general hurry, and we felt quite confident that if the matter had received that share of fair and open consideration which it deserved, those direct discriminations would be removed. They were very bad; business could not be carried on under them. _ There is one thing I want to add to what my hon. friend has said historically. He says that he does not exactly know why Canada in 1920 acted under the three months' notice clause. Of course, the House will recollect that France denounced the treaty, and then said that it might stand-that she wanted to take a general survey of the situation, and that the treaty might stand subject to three months' notice at any time. We gave the three months' notice because the treaty was not doing France any good and was doing us a great deal of harm. We gave notice because under the favoured nation clause Japan, Switzerland and other countries in whose markets we had no direct advantage were reaping the benefits of the treaty. The sale of silks and the like had been largely transferred from France to Japan, which country was doing a great business in silks. Switzerland was also doing a great business in embroideries. The country needed the revenue. And so the notice was given. But after giving the notice the matter was immediately taken up with France for the purpose of arriving at some fair and proper basis under which the business of both countries could be materially advanced.
France-Canada Convention

I want to go further, I want to say that even at the last session of this House, so convinced were we that something ought to be done that from my place in the House I urged that the government send the Minister of Finance over to France for the purpose of making an agreement. I am sorry I ever said a word, very sorry. When I urged that, I thought that one of those planks in the platform of 1919 would not be overlooked. I had thought that luxuries were going to be taxed, that there would be a general large increase on luxuries, and that a cut would be made in favour of France. But I was wrong, absolutely wrong. It used to be a Liberal doctrine, not practised, I admit, that luxuries should be taxed, and heavily taxed. That was endorsed, in 1919, but again the party is in office and it is not practised. Hon. gentlemen will remember that when the former leader of my friends to my left left the government in connection with the budget in 1919 he made the declaration that his interest in connection with customs and excise was to cut down the cost of living, to make cheap the necessities of life, and he wanted a heavy increase on luxuries-make them as high as you can. Why, this country during the war period, just at a time when every single cent of revenue was required, when we put a 7\ per cent increase on all articles coming through the customs, with one or two exceptions-anthracite coal, I think, was an exception-had to except luxuries, which instead of paying 7i per cent extra should have paid a tremendously increased percentage at that period; and she had to do that simply because of the French treaty negotiated by my hon friend in the year 1908.
This treaty, so far as we are concerned, does absolute violence to the principles both of the Progressive and Liberal parties, for it is a treaty cutting down the duties on luxuries. Now I am just going to give }'ou one or two items. Take the first schedule, and what do we find?
Oh, oh.
My hon. friends may laugh but it is hard to get away from facts. We used to have denunciations of this kind of thing ad nauseam from hon. gentlemen opposite in other days, but-
If this treaty facilitates the sale of Canadian products in France surely that is a matter of interest to those to whom my hon. friend is directing his remarks?

I entirely agree with the hon. gentleman. There is some good in everything, there is a little good even here;
I will come to that later. I was not addressing myself to the question of the sale of these articles. I was just pointing out that there was one way in which this thing could have been done easily and properly:	All those
rates could have been very properly increased against other nations and then cut down in favour of France. It is the preference that sh : wants.
Mr. MACDONALD How would you make a treaty?
My hon. friend asks how I would make a treaty. Well, I do not know-
Oh, oh.

-how my hon. friend would make a treaty. I do not exactly know how the United States made their arrangements. I do not exactly know how it is that they have got all of these tremendous advantages that Canada wTas denied. But seeing that the hon. gentleman knows so

France-Canada Convention
much about the matter perhaps he can tell how it is that the United States gets so much advantage, while Canada gets so little.

When was the
treaty negotiated between the - United States and France?

I have no doubt that if the hon. gentleman had properly followed the remarks of the Minister of Finance he would have known all about it. I think the decree that was referred to by the Minister of Finance was the decree of March, 1921 which gave these special privileges to-

Who was in
power then?
In France?
No, in Canada.

Does my hon.
friend really think we were a party to it? If he does not what sense is there in asking such a question?
Now I want to deal with another aspect of this luxury question. After all, this is an agricultural country. We can raise fruits, fcr example. Last year our imports of fresh dried and prepared fruits was over $29,000,000, and a special low rate affecting these is given by schedule D, I think item 105. We grow vegetables in Canada, and we have canning factories in this country, and last year our imports of canned vegetables amounted to $6,400,000. AYell item 86, schedule D, gives a fixed rate of H cents especially to France. We have fishery products in Canada. We import fishery products to the extent of over $3,000,000: and item 120, schedule D, gives special fixed rates, lower than in the case of of her countries, to France. Of animals and their products the importations amounted to over $46,000,000; and item 8, of schedule 1 gives a rate of 29 per cent on:
Canned meats, canned poultry and game; extracts of meats and fluid beef, and soups of all kinds.
Of silks and silk products the importations last year amounted to only $21,000,000; in 1920 they reached a total of over $34,000,000. And hon. gentlemen know the special rates that are given. AVe have the same thing in connection with ribbons and the like. Of books and periodicals we imported, I think, twelve millions. Then novels and works of fiction, advertisement printing matter also get special rates. Therefore I say, Mr. Chairman, if my hon. friend ever wants to adopt any fiscal policy which is going to help production in Canada this treaty is going to make it somewhat more difficult for him to deal with the question.
Now, the Minister of Finance tells the committee that the minimum tariff which he gets from France covers most of our important items. I want to go over a list of those items and see whether we can agree with the hon. gentleman. I am going to take what he thought were important items when the treaty of 1908 was brought in. There are two lists under the treaty-there is the minimum tariff list, and then there is the other list which gives the percentage of reduction in the general tariff of France. Now, these are the items which are taken from the minimum list, and put into another list where they do not get anything like the same advantage:	Oxen,
cows, bulls, steers and heifers, poultry, fresh meat, pork and beef. I ask my hon. friend if those imports are not important. I think that he will say they are. Going further down the list we find: Salted meats, pork, beef and other meats, animal fats, tallow, condensed milk, milk condensed with the addition of sugar, milk food with the addition of sugar, salt, butter and honey. AVhy, Mr. Chairman, all those things are matters of most vital importance to the agriculturists of this country. They are all matters for which my hon. friend got the greatest assistance in his last treaty. They now take second place. Fishing industries are similarly looked after Take the item 47-fish, preserved by pickling or otherwise prepared are also put down. Then item 74: malt and groats, grits (coarse flour) pearled or clean grain; then pulse and potatoes, lupuline, clover seeds and so on-a long list of agricultural articles which in the old treaty came under the minimum tariff, having the right to go into France at the lowest possible rates but which are taken from that list and put in the higher list. I hope my hon. friend will show us why all these products are so treated. Then my hon. friend says that the minimum tariff is absolute as against the world. That has already been discussed, and I think it is pretty clear that it is not absolute as against the world, because the United States can get better terms, and Belgium, Switzerland, Italy and others-and Germany, of course, can get better terms. Then he says that if the United States can get better terms-well we are to get the same. My hon. friend did not say that while the United States gets everything for nothing from France, Canada has to give value-if the States get anything more, well, Canada can have it, but must pay for it. That is the whole extent of that particular concession as you will find in reading the provisions of Article 5.
But the great, objection I see to the whole of this treaty is that France does not agree

France-Canada Convention
to maintain any specific rates at all.	She
gives no specific rates on any article.	She
preserves her tariff autonomously. France does more than that. France does not say that a minimum tariff shall be preserved at all, or that the general tariff shall be preserved as it now is, and of course it is perfectly clear that the only benefit we get under this treaty is the difference that there is between the minimum tariff and the general tariff. There is no obligation on France at all. On the other hand, my hon. friend gives specific rates of duty. He ties his hands and he ties the country's hands. Further, not only is he content that there shall be this maximum list that France can always get, but he goes further and covenants on behalf of Canada that the percentage of difference between the intermediate and the general tariff shall be maintained, so that the benefit that France gets can never be taken from France under that treaty, because this is positive, and her favourable percentage is preserved. We get no positive list, and we have no covenant that the present tariff rates are to be preserved. In any percentage that we get we have no covenant that it is to stay there for any time at all. Now, I put it to hon. members in this way: Let us forget the present position of things in Canada and let us suppose that everything is right-and, of course, the condition of things that we have to-day merely emphasises it-and that we have lots of money and lots to give away. As a matter of principle, where ought the heavy taxes to be? Ought they to 'be on wool, or ought they to be on silk? Ought they to be on lace or ought they to be on boots? Can there be any question as to these things? And if we are interested, as I think we all are, in getting such an adjustment of the tariff as will keep things going properly in Canada, we will make it bear the least heavily on those who can least afford to pay, those who are least interested in luxuries and the like. What do hon. gentlemen think of the treaty, brought down to-day, which deals with two items-I will just take, two though there are lots of others-the items of laces and the item of wool, and makes a reduction of the intermediate on wool? Oh, yes, it makes a reduction there of 15 per cent, and it cuts down the intermediate tariff on wool from 35 to per cent, and yet fixes a duty of 15 per cent on laces. Now, that is the manner in which one of the most important questions which we have to consider and can consider in connection with our national prosperity is treated.

On the other question I agree with my hon. friend that he has removed the disabilities from a large list of articles. There is no doubt about that. There is no doubt that in some instances we have a very real interest in the question. I have no doubt some of these items will prove of some account-largely so.	I think there is an awful
lot of padding in the list, but there are some real items. I am going to ask my hon. friend to let us know just what this treaty means in dollars and cents. In the first instance I think the House ought to have information as to the bank rate, as to what the French rates are, having regard to these different items. We have not got that. I also think that we should have information- and I have no doubt the minister has such information, because no doubt he has looked into this matter before making the treaty- as to the amount of business done under the different items, so that the House will be in a position to consider their relative importance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The requests of my hon. friend appear to be reasonable. And so far as may be possible, I shall be happy to obtain the information. As regards one or two other points on which my hon. friend has spoken, I should like to make a few remarks. First, he tells us that we are reducing the taxes on luxuries, and he mentions a long list. Does my hon. friend not know that the French are producers largely of luxuries? Does he not know that the products of France include wines, silks, embroideries, perfumery, and if we go to France and say: "We shall have nothing to do with you on the basis of luxuries," they will tell us: "You had better go home,"-for you cannot make a treaty with France unless you make some concession to her on the things that she has to sell.

Is there any reason why my hon. .friend could not have put into force the doctrine of his party in 1919,-greatly increased the customs rate on those luxuries and then given the French the proper preference?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not want to discuss questions of past policies; my hon. friend and I would hardly agree on those matters. I want to make this treaty understood by the House, and to get it through as I think it should be put through. But I point out to my hon. friend that France produces these luxuries, and if we go to France and say: "We will not make a treaty with you and make any concession on those things," France will tell us to go home. If my hon. friend admits

France-Canada Convention
that we want to make a treaty with France, he must admit that we must be prepared to give France a concession on the things that she produces. Is that not reasonable? My hon. friend says that we have reduced the duties on luxuries. He complains that we have reduced the duties on laces. In the next breath he condemns us because we have reduced the duty on woollen goods.
No.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes, my hon. friend complained that we are going to reduce the duty on woollen goods.
I was pointing out the small contemptible reduction from 39 to 29J per cent on wool as against a rate of 15 per cent on laces.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does my hon. friend think that we should have reduced the duty on woollen goods to a lower figure?
What I think is that my hon. friend should have increased his general rate on luxuries to a very high figure, and then given France just as much preference on it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We are not dealing with the general rate at all; we are dealing with a treaty with France. I understand that my hon. friend is complaining that we reduce the rate on luxuries, and I say that unless you make some concession on those luxuries which France produces, you cannot make a treaty. My hon. friend knows that is a fact, and that in past negotiations that is what has occurred. I should like him to face this question squarely-if he complains that we have not reduced the duty on wool enough, does he think we should reduce the duty on wool to a lower rate?

I do not mind answering my hon. friend's question at all. I remember a time when he reduced the duty on wool under the British preference, but he found that he was destroying Canadian industry, and accordingly he increased those duties again. He went into that question; he ought to know. But I still say that my hon. friend could have got just the same results if he had raised the duties on these luxuries.
That is not an answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am afraid my hon. friend's answer is not convincing; but if he wants a discussion on the question of destroying industries of this country; if he wants a comparison between the condition of Canada under a Liberal administration and the condition when the Conservatives were in power, if
he will spend an evening some time, we will take up the subject, although the comparison may not be to his liking as regards the story of destroying the industries of the country.
I do not want to go into the past; but my hon. friend almost tempts me. Has he forgotten the picture presented by Sir Charles Tupper when he spoke of the sorrowful wail of the manufacturers of Toronto and Montreal rising up to protest against the tariff? He is repeating these to-day about destroying the industries of the country.

I really must ask my hon. friend not to put words into my mouth. What I said to my hon. friend is this-and I want him to correct me at once if I am wrong-under his original British preference he put in a rate in connection with wool in favour of Great Britain, which rate he himself increased afterwards because he found that the woollen industry in this country was being hurt.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend means that if I find a defect in the tariff I am willing to correct it, I plead guilty at once.
And cover it up.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And cover it up, all right. My hon. friend then pointed out that under the former treaty some articles were under the minimum tariff, and he said: "But you do not have them under the minimum tariff to-day." That is true, but the world has moved since 1907. Many things have occurred since then to change the policy of the French government, and they will not make as generous a treaty to-day as they did in 1907. We have to meet the French government on their ground or come away and not meet them at all. When my horn friend admits that we ought to cultivate trade with France, he must admit what follows-that unless we make a concession on the things in which France is interested it is nonsense to talk about making a treaty. In 1921, my hon. friends opposite made a treaty with France and curiously enough, j-ou find my hon. friend contending to-day that things which were in the minimum tariff in 1907 ought to be in the minimum tariff to-day, but under the treaty of 1921-
Temporary for four months.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
One of the headings in that treaty is "goods that are no more under the operation of the minimum tariff." He had to recognize the changed condition of France and transfer articles from the minimum tariff

France-Canada Convention
to a higher rate. The world has moved since 1907. My hon. friend admitted the movement in 1921, but he evidently thinks that it stopped in 1921. The French policy in that respect has changed, and we have to face that changed condition. Our own tariff is in some respects changed, and we could not go to France to-day and say: "Everything we had in 1907, we are prepared to take to-day." The world has moved. In that respect my hon. friend had to admit that the minimum tariff could not be maintained in regard to some things, and we have had to make the same admission.
My hon. friend has mentioned silks, laces, works of art, perfumery. I want to emphasize the fact that you cannot make a treaty with France unless you are willing to make some concession on those articles that she manufactures. If my hon. friend takes the ground that there should be no concession on those things, he takes the ground that there should be no treaty. My hon. friend says that the United States gets something for nothing. How long they will get those concessions, I do not know, and we are not responsible for what the United States get. "Oh," he says, "we have to pay for them." How are we to pay for them? By reducing the taxes of the Canadian people.
On luxuries.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: By reducing the duty on articles which the Canadian people want to receive. I do not mind making a reduction of that kind when the revenue will stand it, and when it will not hurt our own industries. That is in line with the long-declared policy of our government.

I should like to asi my hon. friend a question and if he has not the information to-day, he can give it to us later. Can he say what countries under the "most favoured nation" clause will secure the privileges that are set forth in schedule D, for instance, regarding items 178, 82, 220 and so forth?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Whatever rates we give to France in any respect under this treaty, we are prepared to give to the "favoured nation" countries. I read a list of them a little while ago. They are Argentina, Colombia, Denmark, Japan, Norway, Sweden, Switzerland and Venezuela. Russia was in, but I leave her out now, and we may practically put in Italy because she will be in this under the new treaty.
Why does the minister leave Russia out?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: All treaties with Russia ended, and I do not know what is to be the future of our negotiations with Russia. She is no longer under treaty with us.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On all matters relating to any change in the tariff I can only say that any suggestion offered will receive our careful consideration and will be dealt with one way or the other at the proper time.
I am not asking the minister to give a decision now; I am only calling his attention to the matter. He has his adviser with him and this is a matter that should be taken into consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I promise at once, unqualifiedly, that it will be taken into consideration. In regard to item 581 my hon. friend seems to think that we are doing something to hurt a Canadian industry. But I am

advised that the class of goods mentioned in that item is not made in Canada at all.

That company has been in operation about a year, and the industry in my own city has been operating now between twelve and fifteen months.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can assure my hon. friend that the matter was carefully thought out, and he will find that my statement is substantially correct, that in this particular case the article is not made in Canada and the item will not affect any Canadian industry. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On item 581?
Yes, item 581, which I have referred to.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall of course be glad to receive any such information, but still I think my information is substantially correct.

I certainly cannot accept that statement of the minister, because I can furnish the name of the firm in Quebec which is making the woven silk, and of the firm in my own city which finishes and dyes the woven goods.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can only ask the hon. gentleman to await further investigation.

I could not help but wish, when the minister (Mr. Fielding) was displaying such manly vigour in his address, that he had displayed some of the same preparatory to making the treaty, and indeed in the negotiations. I want to make, not a lengthy nor a detailed statement by any means, but a summary analysis of the treaty. The minister has come back again with a reference which he said was made by Sir Charles Tupper in 1897, having to do with the tariff which was brought down that year. I do not know that I have ever heard the minister make a speech in parliament in which he has not made this same reference, never making it correctly, never stating the whole of the facts, and always seeking to leave the impression that the tariff which actually went into effect was preceded by predictions on the part of Sir Charles Tupper such as he mentions this afternoon. The fact of the matter
is that the minister, when he made his tariff in 1897, suffered from the same paucity of information that he suffered from in making this treaty with France. When he mads his tariff in 1897 he appeared to be totally unaware-indeed, he was unaware, as the answers to questions in the Commons clearly showed- that the concessions he was then giving in the British preference he was bound to give, under treaty obligations, to very numerous countries in the world, and those concessions were of tremendously greater importance than what he was doing in the way of strict British preference. The consequence of what was brought to his attention in the course of the debate was that the minister later, months later, went back and succeeded in having a provision made whereby the weight of these favoured nation obligations was not only reduced in the main, but mostly wiped away, and the tariff as respects which the predictions were made really never came into permanent operation or anything like permanent operation.
The minister tells about industries flourishing under his government. Did they flourish under the tariff promised in the Liberal convention of 1893? Or did they flourish under the tariff of 1879, by denouncing which the hon. gentleman got into power?
I venture to say now that though there will be instances, due to the oversight of the minister, of manufacturers suffering under this treaty, the man taken care of best is the manufacturer of this country, while it is the rest of the country that is allowed to suffer. And I venture also to append this, that if any of the concessions given France now bear down on those who actually were behind the minister in the contest of 1921, it is the consequence of an oversight and was never intended on his part. He comes to the House and says he has secured a better entrance for Canadian products into France. Canada suffered because of a discrimination which France had imposed against us; Canada came under the incidence of a greatly increased French tariff. The United States had a treaty with France, the effect of which was accentuated by the French decree of March, 1921, and became entitled to a lower tariff than we. Of course, they being our great competitors, that put us under a disadvantage. All this is quite correct.
The United States got those concessions apparently without any quid pro quo on their part. They enjoy them to-day without any quid pro quo. I do not think the United States are entitled at the hands of France to better treatment than is accorded this Dominion, and if the case had been fairly and

France-Canada Convention

strongly presented to the French government, I do not think that government would have persisted in maintaining a situation under which our chief competitors got tremendous advantages over us. I believe^France recognizes that every act of friendship this country has ever had opportunity to display has been shown to that republic. I believe France recognizes that the United States have at no time in their history shown more affiliation for France than we have. I think she recognizes that the friendship of this country is important to her, and I see no reason in the world why on a mere argument of justice and right we should not have prevailed on the French government to give us the same tariff as is given to the United States. That being done, then what we were after would have been secured.
Now, the minister according to his claim- and I think he is right so far as I have been able to examine the treaty-has placed this country, in respect to some of our exports to France, in the same position as the United States. But he has given in return for that concessions which not only tie our hands in framing our Canadian schedules, but which throw out of line vast sections of our tariff, making it compulsory on this country to impose heavy duties upon necessaries that we must import, and at the same time putting at a very low level indeed the duties on luxuries that ought to be taxed away above the levels of necessaries.
The minister says in explanation: I had to put low duties upon luxuries because those are what France sells. I know those are what France sells. That is where the minister went wrongly about his task. He had his tariff in a position where he was not able to bargain at all. France had her tariff in a position where we had to go to her and say: We want to be put on a level with the United States, and if you insist we pay, we will do so. And we have certainly done it. We have placed the duties on silks, velvets, brandies, champagnes, laces, toilet goods, perfumes, and similar, luxuries at a level away below the duties on woollens, cottons and all those other essential imports on which the duty ought to be the lowest consistent with the continuance of the industry of producing them in this country. Not only has he done that, but he has put the grape farm producers of this country-not a few, but thousands of them-in a position where they cannot compete. But he intimates in the House to-day that when the budget comes down he may, by reducing the excise on wines, restore them to a position where they will be on an equality with their com-

petitors in France. There is another concession he has to make, and he is not around the circle then. He will have to keep on reducing the revenues of this country on the very things we ought to get revenue from, reducing them item after item in order to pay for securing what the United States got for nothing. There should first have been a revision of the tariff, when France raised her duties as she did. The revision of our tariff which last session we were in a position to make because we knew then definitely the position of the American government and the position of the French government,-that revision should then have been undertaken, a revision that would have enabled the minister to go to France and maintain at a high level the taxes on luxuries and still give a preference to France that would have at least secured all he has secured by means of this treaty.
Not only that, the concessions he has given mean vastly more than what he fully discloses to the House. I venture to suggest
5 p.m. that under this treaty he has given just about as much concession to Japan, if not indeed more than he has given to France, and he gets nothing from Japan at all. He has given a concession to Japan on silks and other importations, of which we get large amounts from Japan, which will be very serious for our revenue, and which on other goods will be serious as well in respect of Japanese competition.
I will give another instance where the minister went unarmed and returns even now without any appreciation of the bargain hi has made. It will be observed that in respect of articles on which we get the French minimum tariff, France has reserved a right to give to French dominions and protectorates a better tariff than we get. No objection, of course, can be made to that. I would expect the minister to grant that reservation. That is all right. We do likewise in this country in lespect to Great Britain and any other nation of the Empire that gives us like concessions.. But the treaty goes on to make a reservation in respect of any economic arrangement France may enter into with "border states,'' and the minister seems to feel that that makes no difference. Why, he says, that only refers to a small strip along the border which for trading purposes is considered virtually as part of France, and he says a similar reservation was embodied in the previous treaty. Yes, what he has described was embodied in the previous treaty. But what was embodied in the previous treaty is not here. The previous treaty provided-I have it before me-that

France-Canada Convention
there should be a reservation on the part of France in respect to goods granted the minimum tariff applicable not to border states, but applicable only to fifteen kilometres on each side of the boundary. The minister has not incorporated that restriction in this treaty. All the border states may make treaties with France and secure a minimum away below our minimum or France may give them lower duties without any treaty at all. Such reservation applies to Spain, Italy, Belgium, Germany, Switzerland-all those countries are excepted.
France reserves the right to make treaties with all her border states giving them duties below the minimum that we get on this narrow list of articles; she reserves the right to make treaties with her own protectorates on a lower basis; and she reserves the right as well to make treaties with the countries with which she has been at war, for purposes, it is true, of securing goods by way of reparation But although such may be the purposes, the effect is just the same so far as we-are concerned. All those countries may have lower tariffs with France than we get under the very best of this treaty. Such is the prize which the minister comes back with. It is for this that we fix our duties on thirty-one lists of articles of luxury at a very low minimum, the lowest, I think I may safely say, that we have ever had in this country, We have fixed them permanently there as long as this treaty lasts. Whereas those lists in the old treaty contained only twelve classes of luxuries, their number is raised to thirty-one by this treaty, against which we do not get admitted to the French minimum tariff a list anything like as effective as we got under the old treaty.
There is besides the extensions of these concessions which naturally this country has to make arising out of our favoured nation treaties with the nations named by the hon. minister. Now that is what the minister comes back with, and it is not very satisfactory, L think to this country. At best, even with all these reservations, he has noth ing save what the United States, our chief competitor got for nothing, and he has given in-return away beyond what we gave for far greater results in years gone by.
