speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
In reading the discussions in Hansard for a number of years before I had the honour to come before this House, I noticed there was always a long and interesting discussion surrounding the appropriation with respect to experimental farms. Last year, it will be recalled that we had the same experience, and I remember that there were a number of features around which the discussion centred. For instance, what was to be the future of our experimental farm system? Had it any new objective? Were we going to establish any new experimental farms? There were a number of other questions of that nature. I think the discussion at this time might be facilitated and, perhaps, expedited if I made a brief statement with respect to our objective as regards the future of these farms.
Since the House prorogued last summer, I took the opportunity of visiting a large number of these institutions between here and the Pacific coast and also within the province of Quebec. Time would not permit my extending that visitation to the Maritime provinces; but outside of that I visited nearly all the experimental farms. The policy that I partially announced last year was, that before we spend very much more money in the establishment of new experimental farms, the government would be well advised to take care of the existing farms. During the last eight years, four of them being the war period and four since, our experimental farms, of necessity, had more or less to, mark time. That was due to no one's fault; but as a matter of fact, while that is so, the very policy of standing still meant, in some respects, as regards some of the farms, a going back. No growing institution can stand still; it must either go forward or go back. Having regard to that fact and having visited many of the farms, I am more than ever convinced that our policy should be to put the present twenty-two branch farms, including the central farm, in a state of good repair and efficiency before we extend this system to a larger number of farms, particularly in view of the fact that we have not at our disposal sufficient money to do both at the same time.
As regards some of the older farms concerning which there was a good deal of discussion last session, particularly with respect to those on the prairie and the initial four farms,

Supply-Experimental Farms
that is the Nappan farm, the Brandon farm, the Indian Head farm and the Agassiz farm in British Columbia, which four farms with the central farm constituted the original unit, some of these farms, as well as some additional ones, have largely exhausted their experimental work in connection with cultural methods. When I say largely, I do not mean entirely. For instance, the farms at Indian Head and Brandon have pretty well demonstrated to those areas on the prairies just what kind of cultural methods are necessary to get the best results. Forty years ago, the prairies were a secret to most people as regards the best methods of cultivation in order to get the best results. We have blundered on from year to year until many of us have found out something about that great country. The experiments and experience of individual farmers plus the experiments and experience of those experimental farms have blazed the way towards reasonably good cultural methods.
So, to-day, in the light of present conditions, in the light of world demand for high class products, especially live stock products, it is well at this time to extend the activities of those farms more than ever before in the direction of live stock production. In the history of Canadian agriculture, there was never a time when the export demand for live stock products was more difficult and hard to please than it is at the present time. We are competing with highly developed and specialized countries in the production of practically all our meat and dairy products. There is one staple article upon which I think Canada has the edge upon the rest of the world, and that is the production of hard wheat. That we get by nature, due to no particular ability on the part of ourselves, but to the soil and climatic conditions of the West. With respect, however, to live stock and live stock products, we have to compete with specialized countries such as Denmark, Ireland, New Zealand, Australia, Argentina and other countries. Consequently, at this time, the activities of, especially, the older experimental farms should be extended in the direction of more attention to live stock. I think the time has come when we should make these farms largely live stock breeding depots, so that the adjoining territory may be more conveniently supplied with breeding stock from those centres. Possibly, at times, one might be able to establish regular sales of live stock at those centres to which breeders could come in order to secure their requirements.
In visiting the farms in British Columbia, I found, of course, an entirely different condition of affairs. While they are interested in live stock, they are primarily interested in dairying, poultry raising and fruit growing. I did not visit the farm at Invermere, although it was my intention to do so. It is not very easy to get at, and a good deal of time is required to give it the attention it should receive. Possibly at some subsequent date I may be able to visit that farm. But I visited the farm at Summerland on Okanagan lake, and there I found the question of irrigation was one of the uppermost problems. They had difficulty in regard to the supply of water. They were endeavouring to irrigate without the necessary available supply of water, and that question confronted, not only that experimental farm, but many private farms throughout that district. Then there were the questions of fruit growing, of cover crop, of extending the area to be devoted to farming, of what manurial agency should be supplied to the land there, of raising the necessary live stock. I found that one of the problems, a problem which may sound strange to prairie farmers, was to get the necessary quantity of straw to supply bedding to their live stock, two carloads of which they usually fattened during the winter months. Straw cost them from sixteen dollars a ton laid down at Summer-land, and to buy manure from the live stock yards at Calgary would cost them six or seven dollars a ton, so there they were confronted with the difficulty of growing live stock on an experimental farm in that irrigation area. Notwithstanding that, however, they have found it profitable to fatten live stock every winter. Even at the expense of buying dear straw, they found that more economical than not to have any live stock and to have to buy manure from the stockyards at Calgary.
Going further to the West, visiting one of the old initial farms, the Agassiz farm, we found conditions there, from an artistic and a horticultural standpoint, particularly interesting. It was like an old-established farm in some of the more beautiful parts in old England. The shrubbery and trees resembled old country plantations because of their variety and luxuriance.
We found that dairying and poultry raising were given exceptional attention there, and I ran across the cow that subsequently proved to be the world-beater in the matter of producing butter fat. This particular Holstein cow was about half way through her twelve months' period of test, and at that

Supply-Experimental Farms
time, while not making a record with respect to milk production, she promised to be a record maker and breaker with respect to butter fat. The end of the twelve months' period with respect to that cow showed a test for the twelve months of 1345 pounds of butter fat, which is equivalent to 1683 pounds of butter. This is the largest amount of butter fat and butter produced by any single cow we know of in the entire world. This shows what British Columbia can do in dairying; because it would be impossible for any cow to make such a favourable record if the natural conditions were not propitious.
Last year I tentatively intimated that I should like to carry out what seemed to be the policy of my predecessor in regard to the location of an experimental farm on the Canadian National line somewhere between Prince Rupert and Fort George. We found a number of localities suitable for such institutions; and in my opinion, when that part of the country is supplied in this respect, it should really have two farms to meet the situation. However, there may be a difference of opinion with regard to that. After returning to Ottawa and getting down to the preparation of these estimates, however, I found that for another year or two we would have to abandon the prospect of establishing a new farm in that district, although when we do establish one I think that is where it should be located. It is not a very good practice to make too many forecasts, because we have such financial limitations to face. But some day we shall be extending the number of our experimental farms, and I have no doubt that this locality will receive one. My predecessor T of the same opinion, as, I understand, are all the members of the departmental staff.
Coming back by way of Edmonton I visited the Lacombe and Lethbridge farms, which are doing excellent work. At Lethbridge they are also taking up the question of irrigation. This is a comparatively old farm and is well established being in the heart of southern Alberta. It is situated in one of the driest places possible in the West, but notwithstanding that fact, and independent of irrigation, it has shown splendid results this year. With irrigation, of course, the results arc greater still. On all of these farms a great deal of attention is being paid to live stock, particularly dairy cattle. Not only at Lethbridge and at Lacombe, but throughout that part of the country, the inquiries that come from the public would indicate that the farmers generally are in quest not only of live stock but of better live stock. Every superintendent I interviewed reported that when a man was making an inquiry for a brood 
sow he would always specify an animal of the bacon type. This shows that the farmers realize that if they are to compete in the British market they must produce as good an article as little Denmark and Ireland.
I visited one of the newer farms at Scott and also the farm at Swift Current. Swift Current is the last acquisition to the chain of experimental farms and was established two years ago. It also is located in the very centre of the driest part of Saskatchewan, and despite that fact it is showing excellent results. It has been demonstrated there that with very small precipitation, and with proper cultivation, you can grow crops in spite of the drought. By means of the silo and the culti-\ation of inter-tilled crops, like com and sunflowers, they can produce fodder in any year. It would have to be drier than it has been in the past before you could beat that country in the production of fodder suitable for ensilage purposes. Speaking of fodders, this has been the problem which during the dry years has confronted most seriously the live stock men in southern and southwestern Saskatchewan and southern Alberta. We have had a vote in the estimates in the last three or four years providing for free transportation of fodder to and from different parts of Alberta and Saskatchewan. Under the method of growing tilled forage crops, such as I have described, there should be no necessity for ever resorting to that practice in the future, because we can grow these commodities right at home wherever the land is of such a character that it will retain the moisture when conserved. There are a few areas here and there of gravelly or sandy subsoil to which this does not apply. But throughout that country as a whole, in spite of any drought, there is no reason why these fodder crops cannot be grown. And I do not see how the country out there can get much drier than it is. Some years we do not have more than two inches of rain during the growing season, aid it would have to be drier than that before we should be unable to grow fodder for large quantities of stock.
The farm at Scott is in the centre of a peculiar type of soil. Quite adjacent to it the land is exceedingly heavy, while around Scott it is not so heavy and in some parts is comparatively light, although not so light as not to be able to produce profitable crops. And yet we do not get the same results from the summer fallowing system there that we obtain on any other farm in the prairie region. The results are not as good. It is obvious, therefore, that there are many things to be discovered of a cultural character in regard to that farm, and experimental work along that

Supply-Experimental Farms
line will continue there until we can extract from the soil some of the secrets which it hides.
With respect to the farm at Indian Head, with which I am more familiar than any other part of the country, that having been my market town for many years, I may say that the shelter belts, due to the invasion of tree insects, look rather dilapidated at the present time, especially from the railway. Notwithstanding that, however, this farm has announced a first class herd of dual purpose shorthorn cattle, which is creating a great deal of interest in that former wheat territory. The shelter belts are being renovated, different trees being replanted. I have almost concluded that planting box elder or native maple in the shelter belts in the open plains of the West is a mistake. True, it is still to be found in some places; but there are other trees that will do much better and are less open to insect attacks. Around Brandon we had something of the same experience. When you get further east, .around Winnipeg, the box elder makes a reasonably good tree; but we have several trees that make better shelter belts. At least, so far as the experimental farm system is concerned, we will not plant many more box elders. We are devoting our attention to replanting the shelter belts where necessary. But we shall not have to plant them so extensive-, ly as formerly, because we are giving more attention on the farms to live stock, so that we shall not need so many shelter belts to overcome the soil drifting tendencies which we have had to contend with.
Coming to Jirandon, another of our original farms, I found part of it had been destroyed by the freshets of a year ago. The overflow of the Assinboine river, which occurs at irregular intervals, inundated a very considerable part of the farm and seriously interfered with experimental and general crop production. A tree belt had to be removed, partly because of invasion of insect pests and partly because it was too thick. It demonstrated to us that in planting shelter belts we should select a more permanent tree than the box elder. I did not have an opportunity to visit the Morden farm. In the vicinity is the farm of the late Mr. A. P. Stephenson, in his day probably one of the foremost horticulturists in the West. The Morden farm, although established only eight or ten years ago, is making satisfactory progress. I should like also on my way east to'have inspected the Kapuskasing farm. I passed through there on a Sunday and had not time to wait over. The train stopped, however, sufficiently long for me to see from the railway the work done, although of course in a very cursory fashion.
I could see that where formerly was coniferous wooded land-which as a rule is not very productive land in eastern Canada-luxurious crops either growing or in the stook gave evidence of a fertile soil, and I gathered that the country around Kapuskasing has a great agricultural future.
Coming to this province, I have not had an opportunity of visiting our tobacco farms in western Ontario, but I was able to visit four of our experimental farms in Quebec. That province has often been spoken of as not quite so progressive as some of the other provinces. That just depends, of course, on what we call progressive. I had no thought of using the word in a political sense, Mr. Chairman. I found a very large measure of contentment in that province, and the neat farms nestling close to each other, with their whitewashed outer buildings and cosy homesteads indicated substantial prosperity.

Before we rose for dinner I was endeavouring to describe the workings of the various experimental farms throughout Canada, and I shall continue, beginning with Cap Rouge, which is about twelve and one-half miles from Quebec.
1 have already drawn some comparisons between agriculture in the province of Quebec and some of the other provinces of Canada. Nothwithstanding the small farms in Quebec, at no place that I visited did I see greater evidence of contentment, happiness and thrift than in that province. I do not know whether this can be attributed to the fact that Quebec is noted for small farms and large families, while out in the West we are noted for large farms and small families; but possibly the happy medium between these two would be better than cither extreme. We cannot apply the small farm system to the western prairies, but possibly we might modify the size of our farms and make them more of a self-contained unit, such as we find the farms in old Ontario to-day. I am familiar with the conditions during my youth, and I am also familiar with the glory and the great temptation to go into extensive farming operations. On the large farm, if you hit it right, you can make a lot of money, but on the other hand, if you do not hit it right, you can go broke very quickly especially during these days of deflation.

If my hon. friend has any plan calculated to put these farms in better shape without involving the expenditure of money I am open to receive suggestions from him. There is no royal road to farming, even in the case of experimental farms. Such work involves expenditure for men and for other purposes. The question is, are we going to leave the farms in the condition in which some of them are, or are we going to put them in a fair condition of efficiency so that they may function in the way that the originators of this scheme intended they should function, and undoubtedly they require to function today as they never did before. You would only put Canada on its feet through the medium of the development of its natural resources, particularly farming. These must be developed or else we might as well close up. This is not a question on which we should differ very much from the party standpoint, for this reason: all parties and governments have stood behind this system since its inception. It was started by the Conservative government under Sir John A. Macdonald and carried on by successive governments until to-day, and the testimony not only of those who know the most about these farms, but those who have studied systems elsewhere, both on this continent and in Europe, is that we have got a better system of experimental farms than any other place on this continent. I have had an opportunity of investigating them in Europe also, and while I would not make as sweeping a statement as that, I am convinced they will compare favourably. What are we going to do? Are we going to run them in a cheap way? Some 
of them are sick sisters, it is true. These are the ones we want to build up, and if there is any mesmeric way of getting at the result except spending some money, then I am open to suggestions from any source whatever. I recall that my hon. friend from Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) was desperately anxious about a certain vote last year, when I was trying to get the compensation for animals slaughtered on account of tuberculosis reduced somewhat in proportion to the reduced value of the animals. My hon. friend made such strong recommendations, that in a moment of weakness I yielded to him and restored a portion of the original amount. Now, this question all depends on how it affects one's self. I am going to bring down a bill reducing the amount to wrhere I suggested it should be last year, as compensation for pure-bred cattle, and I will give my hon. friend an opportunity of displaying his ideas of economy when that bill is presented. In the meantime my best thoilfeht is that $200,000 cannot be spent better than in putting our experimental farms in first class shape.

Will the minister indicate just how the pioney should be spent? Perhaps he gave that information before I came into the chamber, but I should like to know' just where that money is to be spent. Is it to be spent at all the experimental farms, or are there certain farms that are going to benefit to this extent?

Let any man go into our fruit areas and tell me if the government is not justified in extending a helping hand to this particular industry. It is more necessary in this than any other branch of farming that I know of, because of the fact that it deals which what I call a perishable commodity, which is not capable of being warehoused for an indefinite period like grain.
Is not marketing and distribution the great trouble with the fruit industry to-day?

No question about that. I will come to that in a moment. We have to-day a large number of cattle that are being, not stall-fed but winter-fed, most of them loose in the yard. Some of our breeders have been conducting these experiments, but they have lost money by it, partly due to the fact that they have not had this product on the market long enough to beat down the Old Country prejudice against chilled meat. We hope to take those animals that have been fed on our farms, grain-finish them in order to give them the best bloom and offset any prejudice they might occasion as a result of the chilling process, try out the experiment of sending so many carloads of chilled meat and so many carloads of live animals to .the British market, and compare results. That is one of the propositions we have in mind, and it is under way as regards preparing our cattle for that market.

I am sure we have all followed, with a good deal of interest, the statement which has been given to the House to-day by the minister in regard to the experimental farms throughout the country. I am inclined, however, to think that when his statement is published throughout Canada, there will be a feeling of disappointment as a result of his explanation regarding this increase of $200,000 which we find in the estimates. There is no denying the fact that the experimental work which has been done on our experimental farms has resulted in great benefit to the country. I would not say that the money has been always wisely expended ; but I must rise to express my surprise

Supply-Experimental Farms
at and my disapproval of the proposed increase of $200,000 in this item, if the increase is, as the minister has explained, to establish live stock depots at those farms for the breeding of live stock to supply adjacent districts. This was the main feature of the minister's remarks to the House on this item. The live stock breeders in this country have experienced a rather trying period during the last few years. The deflation which has taken place in the case of live stock is such that, I think they will view with alarm the fact that experimental farms of this country are going to be used now to operate in competition with Canadian breeders of live stock. Many of our live stock breeders have expended much money in the development of the live stock business in Canada, and after all is said and done, I think every reasonable person will acknowledge that Canada owes more to those importers and breeders than it does to the experimental farms as regards the improvement of live stock. That is only natural. I do not believe it is possible for a government to manage a business as well as a private individual can manage it himself, when he is vitally interested in the success of that business; nor do I think it comes within the province of a government to enter upon a field of industry which rightly belongs to the people themselves. I must protest against this proposed plan of making live stock breeding depots of experimental farms to enter into competition with the breeders of live stock in this country.
If, as my hon. friend says, the usefulness of many of the farms has passed, then close them by all means. Let us practise economy to-day if we can possibly do so, and do not let us continue the work on these farms just because they are in existence. With regard to the Central Experimental farm at Ottawa, I think we must all view with alarm the enormous expenditures that are there being made, not for experimental purposes, but in order largely to maintain the farm as a show place for visitors. I think that the amount which has been spent during the past few years, which runs into millions of dollars, for the labour alone that has been employed on the farm, is not justifiable, especially under present conditions. However, I have risen principally to protest against the government using the money of the people to establish experimental farms to undertake the breeding of live stock to supply the wants of the people, which I contend is a business that rightly belongs to the farmers of the country. I do not think that this move on the part of the government is fair or
has any tendency to encourage agriculture in Canada. Furthermore, the government should not go into this business until they know that they can carry it on as well as private individuals can. And it is generally conceded that no government, I care not of what complexion, is competent to carry on work of that kind as well as it can be done privately. Nor do I think it comes within the province of this government, under the conditions that prevail to-day, to paralyze the live stock industry of the country further by an increase of $200,000 in an item which I think is altogether too large considering the results that have been obtained from the experimental farms.
I was amused to hear the minister tell the committee that in his tour of inspection he had seen, I believe from the platform of the train, the experimental farm located four or five hundred miles from here in the bush in northern Ontario, at Ivapuskasing. The day being Sunday, he could not take a further view of the farm than he was able to get from the station. If you go to the furthest point west in the province of Ontario you will find only a small station for experimental purposes in the growing of tobacco, and I do not know whether the minister proposes to discontinue the growing of tobacco there in order to set up a live stock industry. I should be surprised if he did, because that station, for some reason or other, has been practically self-sustaining and has not entailed any great expense upon the Dominion. Perhaps, however, it will probably be closed, because the minister has intimated that, when any station or farm becomes self-sustaining it has ceased to be useful and it is time to close it. I have protested for several years against the treatment which has been meted out to Ontario in regard to experimental farms. That province has to do the work in this direction itself, while at the same time it contributes largely to the upkeep of the work that is carried on in the other provinces. The live stock industry has been encouraged in the other provinces to a degree, which the province of Ontario has not enjoyed. The minister also states that his department is now going to try to dispel the British prejudice against chilled beef, and that an effort will be made to ship that commodity over to the Old Land to convince the Englishman that it is better than the beef to which he has been accustomed. In view of the removal of the embargo against Canadian cattle, and the fact that ocean rates are now about one-third what they were some time ago, the prospects for the live stock industry are no doubt much brighter than they

have been for some years, and I am surprised that the government at this stage finds it necessary to enter upon any large expenditure in the endeavour to remove this prejudice from the minds of the British people. That argument was not advanced a year ago when the grading of hogs formed a part of the government's programme. But it was agreed we should have to supply the article which the British public demand. I think the minister will have on his hands a bigger contract than he thinks in convincing the Old Country citizen that chilled beef is as good as the meat he has been using, and which we are now in a position to place on the British market. I fear therefore that this money will be largely wasted if any attempt is made to carry out the plan which the minister contemplates. I want again to point out the glaring injustice which will be done to the live stock industry and the breeders in this country if the government attempts to enter upon the breeding of animals with the view of supplying the market in the various parts of this Dominion. This is something that ought to be left to the people themselves, and I will venture to state that the government have not been asked by those engaged in the industry to seek an increased vote for this purpose.

I expected that au objection might be raised to these farms devoting more attention to live stock. These farms have been gradually drifting into live stock activities, especially on the prairies during the last two or three years, and we merely want to accelerate that tendency to meet the altered conditions that face us to-day in agriculture. W'hen the government enters into a business like live stock, or say, seed growing or forestry, experience has shown in the past that instead of hurting it has stimulated private enterprise. Take the nursery farms that have been established throughout the country. When they were first mooted it was thought by the nursery men that they would simply invade the average private man's domain and tend to destroy his business. Now it is found that the activities of the Forestry branch have had the effect of increasing private business. The government sends into a district that has not hitherto taken any interest in the matter a consignment of fruits, etc. The neighbours look on and see the industry develop and immediately they send in orders, if not to the government, to some nursery man, who accordingly finds his business increased. The same is true with regard to seed. The seed merchants of Canada were at first very diffident about the government taking any part in the distribution of seed. Now 
they come here and assist us in organizing and extending our activities, knowing that every new convert we get to better seed means more business to them individually. And the same can be said in the matter of live stock. Every district that is induced to put in a club breeding animal establishes a centre that becomes an example to the neighbourhood, and the result is that in a short time orders are placed with private breeders for pure-bred stock. I can assure my hon. friend (Mr. Sutherland) that while I expected the argument which he has so well advanced, experience in the past has nevertheless shown that similar fears have been groundless in regard to other activities. Not only this government, but the provincial governments in the three prairie provinces have been engaged actively in the distribution of live stock for the last ten or twelve years, and I do not know that a single objection has been raised by any stock breeders out there. Why, I really am at a loss to know what to advance to meet my hon. friend's arguments. Those arguments were common stock fifty years ago. But are we going to revert to that day, and must I take up the time of this committee to meet those ancient arguments?
No.

I have done my best to show that my hon. friend's fears are unfounded. With respect to the experimental farms, my heart did bleed freely last year when he described in such harrowing detail the abuses that had been heaped on good old Ontario. Although she had a majority in the preceding government, yet even during their term of office those abuses were afflicting the province. We have three experimental farms in Ontario-the Central Experimental, which I think is equivalent to two or three average branch farms, the Kapuskasing and the Harrow. The Harrow farm has been conducted for about ten years under lease, but recently we purchased the freehold. That farm has been so successful in developing many acceptable varieties of tobacco leaf that to-day our tobacco makers are using a large proportion of our domestic leaf to mix with their imported tobacco-something that they would have considered wholly impracticable twenty years ago. Our purchase of this farm is a good indication that we do not propose to abandon it. Nor did I say that we were going to convert all our farms into live stock breeding stations. I took the ground that in the fruit areas our activities would be along lines suitable to those localities. My remarks in regard to live stock breeding stations were confined to the Maritime and the prairie

Supply-[DOT]Experimental Farms
provinces, and if anyone with any knowledge of live stock will say on his reputation that this industry does not require developing in those provinces, I am open to receive instructors from him. I say again that our live stock industry has receded from the highest point of efficiency and excellence which it occupied even eight years ago, and as compared with thirty years ago our exportable beef to-day is far below the standard of those years. There is a reason for that which I do not need to enter into here. I hope I have allayed my hon. friend's anxiety, but from my experience last year I have my doubts. I will do my best to remove any objections that may be raised in respect to this policy. The only objection, as I have intimated, came from a gentleman who was not an expert on live stock matters, and he took the same attitude as my hon. friend from South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland); and while the reasons with which he supported his objection looked quite plausible, I have not heard further from him. I wrote him fully in reply and from his silence I must conclude that I have converted him. I hope to have the same experience with my hon. friend.

Mr. Chairman, I feel at some disadvantage in following the eloquent member for East York (Mr. Harris). However, I think I understand something about the purpose of these experimental farms. Some hon. gentlemen seem to be under the impression that our experimental farms should be run at a profit. I have never regarded them from that point of view. The purpose of these farms is to experiment along a great many lines that the individual farmer is not able to attempt. These experimental farms are not established as money-making concerns. I do not know whether the hon. minister has convinced the committee or not, but as a stock man all my life I know that to-day the live stock business in our western country is in a bad condition. We have got to help the live stock business back into a prosperous condition in order to make Canada prosperous. I do not know the policy of these farms all the way through, but I do not feel that it is necessary for these farms to compete in a way that is injurious to our live stock interests. I do not imagine that is going to happen. As a stock man I have seen the time when I very much appreciated the opportunity to go to the demonstration or experimental farm in Alberta and get young bulls. I have done that, and I did not feel that those farms were putting me out of business or competing with me when I did so. I have got better bulls than I could get anywhere else right from those farms, and I got bulls that were bred along the lines
Supply-Experimental Farms

that I wanted. I feel that if the experimental farms continue to do that, it will much more than offset any danger of competition with the stock man. There are many stock men in this country who are discouraged to-day, and Canada cannot afford to have the stock business go down hill. It should be our effort to keep the business up to where it ought to be.
I hold no brief for the government as to the expenditure of this money, but I do feel there is a chance for them to use the increase this year to good advantage on the experimental farms. I should like to impress upon the House that these farms are making money for the individual farmer. I thought I knew the business pretty thoroughly myself, but I have had a good many pointers from the experimental and demonstration farms. I could not afford to do that experimenting myself, but I took advantage of their experiments and applied what I learned to my own farm, to my profit. That is the light in which I look at the experimental farms.
I am not going to enter into any dispute as to whether or not the government will use this money rightly, but I am not here to oppose the government in something which I think it is possible for them to make of service to our country. Agriculture has never had the encouragement and money expended upon it that it should have had, in proportion to the importance of the industry in Canada. I do not care to make a speech on this subject, but I did want to tell the House how I felt about it, and I have been a stock man all my life. If there are other lines in which part of this money is to be spent, the minister has not told us about them; there is plenty of room in the stock business alone to use all that increase, if it is expended in the right way, and I am willing to support the government and give if a chance to make good on this item.

It might be well to point out that this item of $1,525,000 which is credited under the Department of Agriculture is a sum to be spent on experimental farms, which in turn furnish opportunities to each and every individual throughout the whole Dominion. Usually a vote of this nature is supposed to be wholly and solely for the purposes of agriculture, .which represents, we will say, possibly fifty per cent of the people of Canada. But that is an absolutely erroneous view to take of the question.
I would also point out that I have great faith in the present Minister of Agriculture, as I had in the previous Minister of Agriculture, and I have always supported the esti-
IMr. Warner.]
mates brought down by both these hon. gentlemen simply because I have always felt that agriculture in Canada has been starved and has never received its fair proportion of the public moneys that was its right, and was necessary to establish the industry and give it a fair chance as compared with other governmental activities. One of the reasons why I say a complimentary word of the present Minister of Agriculture is because in my own province I had the pleasure of working for him in a small way for twelve years while he was Minister of Agriculture in the province of Saskatchewan, and I know whereof I speak. That is one of the reasons why I do not question his action when he comes to this House and asks for an increase of $200,000 in this vote, because I feel sure that it will be expended wisely.
As I stated before, a vote of this kind will benefit each and every individual in the Dominion if they like to accept the opportunities afforded through the experimental farm system. I do not approve of the idea that it would be economy to cut that off. There is such a thing as false economy, and if you put the number of people who are interested in agriculture at 48 or 50 per cent of the population, this amount is very, very small indeed to be allotted to agriculture. The sum of $200,000 is a mere bagatelle; it is not nearly enough. I stated to the minister last year that under his jurisdiction I would be prepared to stand in my place and ask for an increase of $1,000,000 for the purposes of agriculture this year. I would point to this fact in support of the statement I made when I first rose, that for about five years only the small sum of approximately $3,000,000 was voted in this large Dominion for the purposes of agriculture. I say it was a crying shame that governments in this country should have continued so long to pay so little attention to the merits of agriculture that they allowed it to get along with a paltry $3,000,000. We have protested, and our protests are now being heard At the same time we recognize the extreme importance of keeping down expenditure in this country. But there is wise and unwise expenditure, and I have no hesitation in passing my judgment at this time that this $200,000 is a very wise expenditure, and if any fault is to be found with it at all, it is that it is too small.
Mr. STEED8MAN: I was pleased to hear the minister this afternoon outline his policy of encouraging the live stock industry, particularly in the prairie provinces. I agree with him when he says that permanent agriculture requires the development of live stock. There

is one feature in the development of live stock which I hope the minister will not neglect. While I come from a grain-growing district, I am particularly interested in the development of live stock with the growing of grain. The minister spoke this afternoon about the development of fodder crops, but I would point out that in the territory that he mentioned this afternoon, particularly southern Manitoba, southern Saskatchewan, and southern Alberta, in order to go into the live stock industry we must have something more than the fodder crops that he mentioned. We have not got in that country up to the present time a grass or fodder crop suitable for pasture in the summer or for hay. I refer to southwestern Manitoba. I feel that it is absolutely necessary that some of the money expended on the experimental farms up there should be devoted to experiments along that line. I am convinced that stock raising must come to make agriculture permanent there. Not only do we want development of the live stock industry, but we must have those plants I spoke of in the interests of rotation. We must have a satisfactory rotation of crops that will restore the root fibre to our soil, and in that way prevent the drifting of the soil which is becoming prevalent in the older parts of that country. I would like to ask the minister if he will make a note of that, and see to it that experiments along the line of developing grasses, clovers, and fodder crops shall be continued in that part of the country.

I shall vote with a great
deal of reluctance for any increase in national expenditure, and yet I do not feel inclined to oppose this particular outlay. It is some thirty years since we first commenced to agitate for the British embargo on Canadian cattle. Now when it is removed we find that the British farmer desires our store cattle provided they are of the right type. It is quite evident, I think, that there are great possibilities in this direction, and that we should be able to develop a very large trade if the matter is properly handled. For that reason, knowing so well the Minister of Agriculture, in whom I have, like the member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould), the very greatest confidence because of his administrative ability, having lived in the same province where he successfully handled the department of agriculture, I have decided to vote for this
item but I would like to make two or three comments about the experimental farms.
In the first place I would ask the minister if any plans have been laid down in connection with the raising of pure-bred stock at the farms for so distributing the different breeds that the purchasers will not be under the necessity of paying freight for a long distance. For example, we have two experimental farms, one at Brandon and the other at Indian Head, perhaps raising the same breed of stock-Shorthorns. I do not know that both are doing that, but I know that one is. Then if in another part of the Dominion two farms near together were raising Herefords and in another comer of Canada two farms were raising Aberdeen Angus it could be readily seen that it might be very awkward for those who wished to purchase this breeding stock. It would be better if they were more scattered.
One other comment, and this may seem very strange especially to those who have not been in the stock business, and that is that the cattle that are now being raised on our experimental farms, at least some of them, do not exactly fill the bill, if they are to be regarded as types for the ordinary farm, and for the reason, that they are too well cared for in their young days. We know that animals that have been raised in what I might term a pampered condition and not allowed to rustle for themselves, when placed side by side with cattle raised on the ordinary farm present a very poor appearance, a very sorry sight. I have seen them myself in very poor flesh compared with cattle raised on the ordinary farm under ordinary conditions, although the latter was in splendid condition, and that continues year after year. I remember quite well a conversation with that grand old stock man of Manitoba, Mr. Bedford, in which he stated that one of the great difficulties he had with his cattlemen on the farm was this: They were inclined to keep the windows of the barns always closed and the cattle never were allowed to be out in the cold very much. He said he was always at them to keep the windows open so as to allow the fresh air in, and permit the animals to rough it a little bit. I think every stock man knows that the young stock raised under such conditions when distributed throughout the country and kept under ordinary farm conditions will give very much better results.
These are the only comments I have to make. Perhaps the minister will answer the question I asked him, if there is any plan for the distribution of the various breeds of stock.

We have been asked for some criticisms with respect to our experimental farms. Let me say that I am glad to know that the government have undertaken a new policy. I used to be of the opinion, and still think, that the experimental farms have been following too closely an ancient plan that was laid down several years ago. I am now glad to learn that they are adopting new views, and are going to change the former policy.
The first criticism I would make is that the appropriation for this purpose does not seem to be so arranged that we can discuss it intelligently. What I mean by that is this: Coming from Manitoba I only know, in a general way, what the experimental farms are doing in that province. So far as the farms in the East are concerned I cannot say whether they are accomplishing the results expected of them or not. I appreciate the work that the experimental farms have done and have this to say in regard to the development of our Marquis wheat. The origination of that variety of wheat alone has probably meant more for the Dominion than would be required to carry on our experimental farms for the next hundred years or more. I realize that in experimental work an investigator may labour for practically a life time and finally, when he is almost giving up in the belief that he has accomplished nothing, he makes some discovery which may be productive of marvellous results. I repeat that I fully appreciate the work the farms have done in the past, and any suggestions I may make are advanced in the hope of aiding them to assist our farmers to a still greater degree in future.
In the next place I think there is overlapping between the federal department and the provincial departments. Personally I should like to see the experimental farms conduct their various experiments in the interest of the agricultural industry, and then continue those experiments further and demonstrate that work along these lines could be successfully undertaken on the average-sized farm. So far as I know, in Manitoba at any rate, the experimental farms have not been giving any demonstrations. I would suggest that demonstration stations should be established if at all possible. Perhaps the manager of an experimental farm might get in touch with some of the farmers in the country and persuade them to adopt methods that have been proven to be superior to the ones they are following. For example, he might select a farm that is overrun with weeds, or the soil of which has been impoverished, and there demonstrate some of the conclusions arrived at on the experimental 
farm. I believe this would be a good work to get before the people.
I want to say further that the experiments carried on at the experimental farms do not seem to be known to a sufficiently large number of people. I would suggest that the government by some means induce people to go to the experimental farms and see the work that is going on. So far as the reports are concerned, I do not know whose fault it is. I have no suggestion to offer as to how to get information to the people, but I should say that the information that has been obtained on the experimental farms to-day is not getting to the people, and what is the use of experimenting if the farmers do not know the results. Practically speaking that is the condition of the country. A few who are more energetic visit the farm occasionally, but I think if records were available of the number of people visiting the farm we would find a very small percentage of agricultural people among them. They are more likely to be townspeople, driving out to the farms to see the flower beds, the hedges, the shade trees and so on. I say that I appreciate the work the farm is doing, but I claim that there is an overlapping of the work of the experimental farms: that is the federal experimental farm and the provincial farms. I claim that the work that is being done on the farm should be communicated to more people. It will be of no use to carry on experiments, if the results are not known, except by a few townspeople and the people working on the farm.
Did I understand the minister to say that a certain amount of this grant was for exhibition purposes?

If my hon. friend will allow me, I will answer the question asked by my hon. friend under the gallery, who promised to support the vote if I would give him a reasonable justification for it, and tell him where the money is to be expended. I mil answer the last question first. The sum of $2,000 is to be used for the expenses in connection with the Imperial Exhibition in the Old Country in 1924, for grouping material together for that exhibition. I do not think I need go over all these items, Mr. Chairman, but just for the purpose of giving the House some idea of where the money is going, I may say that I will start down by the Atlantic ocean. Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, is to receive an increase of $6,000 over last year for the purpose of carrying on experimental work on the area recently acquired for

this farm. We acquired 40 acres to supplement the farm that was too small. That has to be developed, fed, and drained. At Nap-pan, N.S., there is an increase of $2,000 for experimental work in marsh lands. This is one of the farms that requires taking care of. As a matter of fact, as I have intimated, they have all had temporary care during the last eight years. At Fredericton, N.B., there is an increase of $5,000 for experimental work in general; at Ste. Anne de Pocatiere, an increase of $2,000 for experimental work; Cap Rouge, an increase of $3,000 for dairy equipment, fertilizer work and work in horticulture; at Lennoxville an increase of $5,000 for experimental work; at La Ferme, Que., an increase of $4,000 for clearing and draining and increased work in horticulture; at Kapus-kasing, Ontario, an increase of $5,000 for experimental work and provision of a second assistant; at Morden, Manitoba, an increase of $4,000 for new roads and fences and additional planting in the orchard; and at Brandon, Manitoba, an increase of $15,000, $12,000 of which is for the purchase of new land, the remainder for an increase of the work in forage crop breeding. That was because of the flooding of the land in the valley of the Assiniboine. We cannot rely upon that district' any longer for experimental purposes. It is liable to break up at any time. Then at Indian Head, Saskatchewan, there is an increase of $5,000 for providing two additional assistants and clearing up the forestry and shelter belts; at Rosthern, Saskatchewan, an increase of $8,000 for expansion of the work in animal and field husbandry, and the appointment of an additional assistant; at Scott, Saskatchewan, an increase of $5,000 for the purchase of feed and appointment of an additional assistant; at Swift Current an increase of $9,000 to complete the work of the establishment of this new farm; and at Lethbridge an increase of $25,000, $20,000 of which is for the purchase of new land for irrigation experiments, the remainder for the carrying on of these irrigation experiments. They have not yet taken up to any great extent the matter of irrigation. They have done it only in a small way. At Lacombe there is an increase of $12,000 of which $10,000 is for the purchase of new land, and the remainder for increased feed for live stock experiments; at Summer-land an increase of $15,000, of which $10,000 is for the purchase of land, and the remainder for irrigation experiments. So it goes on through the list.
In reply to my hon. friend from Neepawa (Mr. Milne): the tall, fine-looking gentleman
who speaks of the necessity of more publicity-

There are very many
that answer that description.

I mean the tall one.
I am impressed with the fact that we know more about farming than we make known and carry out, and that there is a great deal of work done on the experimental farms that a great many of the people never hear anything about. I do not know how we are going to correct that. The reader of to-day is a headline reader rather than a serious reader, who will sit down and read a government bulletin. In spite of that we find some encouragement in the fact that a great many applications are made for bulletins or folders A little bulletin is sent out called Seasonable Hints, published quarterly, and in that will be found an invitation to all and sundry to send in an application for any bulletin that they might be interested in. If they do we will send it to them. The old way was to distribute these bulletins indiscriminately; if you were not in the right humour to read them you threw them into the waste paper basket, and if you were not an active supporter of the government you would not take any stock in them. Now, we send them out on application, and still, in spite of that, we feel that the information does not get to the people as much as we would like. If my hon. friend has any suggestions to make as to how we can make the work more popular, take more advantage of it, have the people read more about our experiments, we would be glad to receive them. I ran across a farmer in Saskatchewan at Christmas time who had put up a silo in my own district where I have live! for forty years. The silo was quite a joke even last year, after some people in other parts of the province had started to use them. After this gentleman had filled the silo with sunflowers he had some over, and he found his cattle ate them, standing in the field. I asked him how it came about that he started to build a silo and experiment with ensilage and feeding the cattle with this fodder that was never heard of before. He said that he had been reading some of the bulletins some guy from Ottawa had sent him, that he had beeome interested in them and that after reading about the matter in various publications he had come to the conclusion that there must be something in it and he tried it.
Who was the "guy"?

He referred to all and sundry that wrote bulletins as " guys But the information he received made him a
