convert to this silo method, and he went into it, in spite of the fact that his neighbours made fun of him, because the feeding of sunflower as ensilage was looked upon as a pretty good joke in a wheat territory. That is the way to get the information. It is just like any kind of missionary work; it takes a great deal of planting to get any harvesting; but nevertheless, the good work must go on. I hope that is sufficiently exhaustive for my hon. friend.
Are there no savings at all anywhere throughout the country?

Does the hon.
member mean in the improvement of these farms?
Were the budgets from any of these particular farms any less than they were last year, and how was the money allocated that came from such places?

I went over them all and they all called for additional expenditures. My hon. friend must realize that not only the experimental farms, but practically every provincial and federal Department of Agriculture in Canada, when the war broke out, simply sat tight and marked time. When that is done for four years and then followed up with a similar procedure during four more subsequent years, one can understand the need for expenditure to put those farms into proper shape.

Does the minister not
remember that last session he told us in this House that he would keep the vote down?

No, that I would keep it down as low as true economy would permit; but good economy and the best kind of economy is sometimes wise expenditure. My hon. friend must have been out of the House before dinner, because he asked me if we were going to establish any new farms and where. I made it quite plain that we were not for the present, until we got the old ones into shape.
The minister is establishing a new farm at Swift Current.

It is comparatively new. It is what we call our baby farm. We sometimes use that appellation in connection with people who are ten, twelve or twenty years old. It is the last farm to be established, it is, comparatively speaking, a new farm. The matter of freight rates and breeding, certain kinds of stock on certain farms is a difficult one. We find the tendency throughout Canada is to introduce too many breeds 
of sheep, too many breeds of swine, too many breeds of dairy cattle, and the more you do that, the greater is the tendency for crossbreeding. The result has been the encouragement by all governments of community stock breeding, to induce groups of farmers to engage in breeding along the same line and with the same breeds of animals. This is cheaper, but it is very difficult to bring it into effect. We shall have to keep, let us say, three standard breeds of dairy cattle in a dairy district. In the Indian Head district with which my hon. friend is more familiar, as I am, we have a dual purpose, Shorthorn breed of cattle. Some people are of opinion that there is no such thing. We have in Brandon, where there is a similar herd, a record of 11,000 pounds of milk annually, and that is pretty good for even a dairy breed. In this way we are doing what we can to encourage community breeding, but it is a hard matter, indeed, to say that we shall not take on, say -three breeds. We are pretty nearly compelled to do so inasmuch as there are three standard breeds of both beef and dairy cattle.	There are two outstanding breeds of bacon hog, if not three. If we could reduce that to one, I am satisfied that we would be further on; but you can hardly get the thing down so fine that you are going to be able to size up just where you are going to save on freight rates to the market from where the prospective demand will come. I have not, at least, been able to work out any policy. The main idea in a district like Indian Head, where the farmers have been exclusively wheat growers for forty years, is to encourage the variety and particular breed of live stock that will be most attractive to wheat growers. I think the average wheat grower would prefer to go into something that would make beef, rather than to breed dairy cattle, or, perhaps, go into hog raising, or poultry raising in preference to that. That is what we have in mind in developing a herd, or a flock as the case may be, at any particular station.
I think an hon. member from Manitoba spoke of the advisability of having more excursions. At Indian Head, that provided some of the best publicity that farm got in the early years. We had regularly organized excursions from all parts of the country. Not only was an excursion a social outing; but many practical lessons were learned, and hundreds and thousands of farmers went away to the open prairie filled with enthusiasm from seeing the homelike surroundings of that farm and what could be done in the direction of tree growing as well as crop growing. I do not know why these excursions have been abandoned.

Supply-Experimental Farms
unless it is because farmers have now become familiar with these farms and because we do a certain amount of illustration work. That is another thing of which my hon. friend spoke. There are a hundred illustration farms carrying on demonstrating what has been accomplished on the experimenal farms. In the province from which my hon. friend comes, I understand there is not one illustration station, and there are none in Ontario. These illustration stations are established on request; we do not force them on the public, because if we did, the farmer who would take the thing up under anything like persuasion, would not be very likely to make a success of it. But if my hon. friend has in view any man who is of an experimental turn of mind, who likes that kind of work, who is already dabbling in it, we shall be glad to do illustration work on his farm on the usual terms. That costs probably three to four hundred dollars per farm per year. We have one hundred of these illustration stations and they are doing a great deal of useful work. They will be accelerated in those districts I have spoken about that are waiting for experimental farms, out on the National Transcontinental between Prince Rupert and Prince George.
Some remarks were made by my hon. friend (Mr. Steedsman), I think, perhaps, as a result of misunderstanding my remarks with respect to the development of forage plants. I merely mentioned sunflower and sweet clover, as extremes, in the development of what was looked upon formerly as comparatively useless plants. That has been a feature in a sense; it has provided the unexpected source; but in addition to that a tremendous amount of experimental work has been done in developing fodders along the line of domesticated grasses. I am quite frank in admitting that I do not know, especially for the dry areas, any recognized grass that will give what we call a catch successfully by seeding down with a crop one year with another, particularly in the drier parts of Saskatchewan and Alberta. If we can develop a dry-land plant that will give us a catch of grass when sown with grain, then we shall certainly have brought about a revolution in the drier parts of Saskatchewan and Alberta and in some parts of Manitoba.
I do not know where we can get such a plant. The nearest approach to it possibly, i3 the sweet clover, and the annual variety is a very promising plant. Many people do not like either of them; but nevertheless live stock get quite accustomed to and fond of them. When stock eat sunflower, they will certainly come to eat sweet clover. A great
deal of work remains to be done in that connection still, I admit; but that only proves that the work of experimental farms is not anything like exhausted yet. I read articles written by young men about a proper rotation including grass, let us say, in Saskatchewan or the drier parts of southern Manitoba or Alberta. I have never seen one worked out successfully yet, although I do not say that that cannot be done. I think possibly some drought-resisting grass may be found; but I think if one is to look for the best results, seeding down of grass in those dry areas must be done alone. That is expensive, and that is the reason why grass-growing and stock-raising has not been as successful as it should be, and has not been tried out as much as it should have been in those districts. That is the reason we turned to ensilage such as I have described, namely, com and sunflowers, because these are annuals and they will grow a crop whether it is dry or wet, the crop being of course better when there is a reasonable amount of moisture. Now I think I have covered all the questions raised.

I have listened with a great deal of interest to the explanation of the minister and to the remarks of different hon. members who have spoken. The minister has given us a long list of increased expenditures embracing various items from $3,000 up to $20,000 in connection with these experimental farms. I am willing to-night and at any time to support any reasonable expenditure for the maintenance of these farms, but I am not willing at this inopportune time to support any undertaking to go into the further development of them when the money market is so bad; and I think that the minister is extravagant in his tastes when he suggests that we ought to vote all this money. The minister made the statement to-night-I do not know whether he .meant it or not-that these farms were already in a high state of efficiency. That being the case, why does he suggest spending $200,000 more, especially after having received an increase last year of $150,000? There are more fads introduced into this department than are being introduced into the schools and colleges in the big cities of this country. And that is saying a great deal. My hon. friends to my left will never vote a dollar for anything in the line of industry, but they are all with one exception willing to vote millions for this particular purpose.
Order.

Well, that attitude has been evident to-night. One hon. gentleman said
Supply-Experimental Farms

that it was a shame to reflect that at one time the department was run with $3,000,000 and he added that it should have been millions more. To-night I think the item calls for $6,000,000 odd. I think that when private individuals are trying their best to cut down overhead expenditures the government should set an example and economize, but how the minister expects the public debt to be kept down when he asks for such increased expenditures as this I cannot see. I have always been a supporter of the men who work on the farms, I am willing to vote money for the improvement of agriculture and I would willingly vote for the expenditure of this increase of $200,000 if the country were as prosperous as it should be. To-night I asked one of my colleagues why it was that we had not been given the details of the item of $1,600,000 and I was told that it would necessitate too much printing. Well, it would have saved the minister a great deal of explanation, and hours of the time of the Home, if he had given those details. So far as my friends to my left are concerned, I think the cheapest thing would be to establish sufficient experimental farms and place upon them all the genuine farmers of that group. At least it would save the time of the House.

I was somewhat surprised at the remarks made by the minister before six o'clock and shortly after recess, in which he said that the department would practically revolutionize the experimental farm system. I have listened with much interest to the statements he has made, and he is now trying to impress upon the House that this increase in the expenditures is to be applied to various branches of work carried on in conection with the experimental farms. Some hon. gentlemen have taken the ground that some one has been criticizing these expenditures because the farms have not been self-sustaining. Now, I do not think that anyone has attempted to criticize the farm's on any such ground. No one expects an experimental farm to meet expenses or to pay profits, that is not what it is established for. The minister suggested a few moments ago that we had too many breeds of live stock in the country and it was necessary to standardize and reduce them. One would almost infer from his remarks that this was one idea which it was intended to put into practice in connection with the live stock depots that are to be established on these farms to supply stock to the farmers. I think he said that we have about three standard breeds of cattle. He mentioned dairy and beef cattle. He might tell us which one 
of the breeds he mentioned will be singled out by the department. I see a danger in connection with any undertaking of this kind. Individuals have invested a great deal of money in pure-bred animals of various breeds and their whole investments may be tied up in connection w?ith the breeds which the experimental farms will not specialize in. In that way there might be material damage done to legitimate and useful business in the country, and this was one of the things I had in mind when I was trying to show the danger that might attend any attempt on the part of the government to enter upon the breeding of animals on a commercial basis to supply the wants of the people. I consider that this is something that should be left to those engaged in the business. I have always encouraged the purchase by the government of the very best animals that could be procured to be kept on the farms as examples to breeders. I was at the Canadian Live Stock Show in Toronto last winter and was particularly pleased to note that the province of Manitoba exhibited the grand champion Clydesdale stallion of that show in competition with other exhibitors. I thought it was a great compliment to the good judgment of the agricultural department of that province in making such a wise selection. But that is an entirely different matter. That exhibition serves a useful purpose as an object lesson to students visiting the place. But it seems that the government in this case intend to specialize in two or three breeds, and I infer from the minister's remarks that he thinks that even three are too many. So far as bacon breeds of hogs are concerned he says that two ought to be sufficient. Well, that may be true, but possibly competition may serve a useful purpose. Competition is the life of trade, and the competition which we have in our exhibitions is one of the most useful things in connection with our agricultural industry. Those who had the privilege of visiting this exhibition in Toronto last winter as well as the great winter show at Chicago must have been favourably impressed with the resources of this country, for we had a magnificent display from every part of the Dominion.
As far as western Canada is concerned, I must say to their credit that many of their exhibitors at the winter show in Toronto secured a large share of the prizes. I think many breeders there of pure-bred live stock will object very strongly to the government entering into competition with them, particularly if one or two breeds are given the preference. I should like the minister to pay a

little more attention to this question and give the committee further light on what he proposes to do, and what particular breeds are to be singled out, because I would judge from his remarks that, like every other farmer, he has a personal preference for certain breeds as being the most useful.
Apparently from his remarks on the feeding of live stock, the sunflower is a new development that our friends from western Canada knew nothing about until a few'years ago, but I am inclined to be a little skeptical as to that.
The Seasonable Hints to which the minister referred, I have found them in banks and other public places through-
10 p.m. out our province in stacks for distribution, with an invitation to the reader to apply to the nearest experimental station for information with regard to agriculture. Unfortunately as far as we are concerned in Ontario, from Ottawa west for five hundred miles the only practical demonstration we can have in agricultural methods is in relation to the growing of tobacco, for we have no other Dominion operated farms. We have fruit growing stations in several parts of the province, but they are maintained and operated by the provincial government. And as far as tobacco growing is concerned, I am afraid that the present labour situation will deter those who might wish to go into that industry.
If the minister would briefly indicate the particular breeds that are to be developed and placed in competition by his department with other breeds raised by the breeders of this country, he will be rendering a service to them by way of warning as to what they are going to be up against in the near future.

I thought I had
already dealt with the question by pointing out to the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Millar) what we are doing at Indian Head. In that heretofore wheat growing district we thought that the dual purpose shorthorn cow would be taken more kindly to because she lends herself both to beef production and dairying. The same may be said with regard to Brandon. At Swift Current and Scott, too, it is generally thought that dairying cattle will be the line of stock developed, especially now that- the silo is a recognized institution in that territory. Quebec is a recognized dairy province, and on most of the farms the dairy breeds will be handled. The three standards I had in mind were the Holstein, the Ayrshire and the Jersey. There are other breeds, of course, but if we take up too many breeds
Supply-Experimental Farms
we are going to dissipate your activities too much to accomplish anything substantial. In the Eastern Townships territory, in the vicinity of Lennoxville, where a considerable number of beef animals are grown, we have the beef breeds established, and the dairy as well in the Ayrshire and the Jersey, giving the farmers their choice. We are not arbitrarily imposing these particular breeds on the farmers in any district-they happen to be the predisposition of the local farmers. We cannot go into a district and say:	Here, you
have been doing so and so in the past, but if you are going to get any benefit from our methods you must change your breed and adopt ours. So far as is consistent with good practice and good business we are trying to meet the wishes of the respective districts with regard to the particular breed they desire to develop. For instance take what is known as the Canadian Jersey or the Canadian cow at Cap Rouge. The people there are wedded to that particular breed and do not want any other. It is an exceedingly good dairy cow, with a certain amount of sentiment attached to it, and it is to-day a registered breed. What would be the use of talking any other breed there? While we do not want to be arbitrary, at the same time we desire to be sufficiently advanced in our policy as to lead in the direction that we think will most effectively meet the reasonable requirements of the people directly concerned.

I am not rising to criticise this vote involving a $200,000 increase, for if the money is well spent I think it will be a benefit to the Dominion as a whole. But I do think that when money is being spent to buy land for new farms the district I represent should get first consideration. The Cariboo district represents about a third of British Columbia. The Minister of Agriculture in the preceding government (Mr. Tolmie) I understand strongly recommended the establishment of an experimental farm along the line of the Grand Trunk Pacific. Last summer I had the honour of accompanying the present Minister of Agriculture through there and we looked over several locations. Not only so, but his deputy, I understand, went through there last fall and definitely located where an experimental farm should be established. The money I might say was voted last year, and when other experimental farms are being purchased I think the least this committee could do would be to re-vote that item for the establishment of a farm in the Cariboo district. There are a great number of returned men in the vicinity of Prince George who
Supply-Experimental Farms

know very little about farming, and they want some one to give them a lead. Seeing that the last government recommended the establishment of a farm along the Grand Trunk Pacific railway and that this government approves of it, I think they are in honour bound to start operations this coming season.

I listened with a great deal of interest, Mr. Chairman, to what the hon. minister had to say before adjournment this evening with regard to the establishment of breeding depots in connection with our experimental farm system, and I am rather anxious to have a little more information on the point. Judging from the term, one would form the idea that it is the intention of the government to breed cattle and to sell them in competition with the live stock breeders of the country. The department has been doing that to a certain extent up to the present time, but as I understand the hon. minister this evening, it is intended to extend that work to a much greater degree. If so, I may say that we have had a little experience as breeders of pure bred live stock in British Columbia in competition with the government in the same line of work. The government, you will readily understand, has a great many advantages over the ordinary breeder. When it comes to attending exhibitions it can put on a large string, and can also stand a much heavier cost than the ordinary breeder would be able to bear. Then again, being a government institution, its advertising is far more extensive than that of the ordinary breeder. It is true that the work carried along these lines will bring buyers from outside points, but these buyers almost invariably go to the government establishments to secure what they want. It would be very unfortunate indeed if the breeders who have done a great deal of pioneer work in this country and spent large sums of money in importing first-class animals should be compelled to meet heavy government competition along these lines, and I would like to have a little more information from the minister on that point.
With regard to inducing people to maintain certain breeds of live stock in certain sections of the country, while I agree that that would be very nice if once it can be accomplished, I can assure the minister that in my opinion he has assumed a very heavy job indeed. In the first place, we have to leave a great deal in a matter of this kind to the intelligence of the breeder himself. The greatest breeding country in the world will probably muster more breeds of horses, cattle, sheep and swine at their public exhibitions than any other country in the world, and that 
is Great Britain. I visited the Royal Show in 1921, and I may say that I saw all the breeds that I had ever seen at exhibitions on this side of the water, and in addition, many breeds I had read of but never seen, and some that I had never even read of-some brand-new breeds that had been created only within the last few years. So that when moving along these lines, a great deal must be left to the intelligence of the individual.
There is another point that must not be overlooked. In a country like Canada where we have about three and one-half million dairy cows, averaging about four thousand pounds of milk a year each, we have a common enemy to compete with, and that is the scrub cow. It does not matter whether the cow we bring in competition with that scrub is a brown Swiss, or a Guernsey, a Jersey, a Holstein, or any other breed, if she will increase the average output of the cows of this country to an appreciable extent she is rendering very valuable service to Canada.
I must congratulate the hon. minister and his officials and also the superintendent of tha Agassiz farm on having produced there a cow with a world's record for the production of butter, a record in competition with all other countries in the world. That record is a very good one indeed, and I think that every tribute should be paid to Mr. Hicks, the superintendent of that farm, for the excellent work he has done in that connection. It only backs up what I have said in this House on previous occasions, that the Fraser river valley with its mild climate and ability to produce various kinds of fodder will be one of the greatest dairying sections of our Dominion.
I am pleased to note, too, that the minister still has in mind the placing of an experimental station in northern British Columbia. I looked over that territory when I was minister and I was astonished at its wonderful expanse and its adaptability for the development of the dairying and general live stock industry. These men are struggling along up there, and the advice which they could obtain through an establishment like a Dominion experimental farm would be exceedingly useful to them, and any money expended in that line would be bound to bring excellent results.
I am not one of those who believe that we can develop Canada by adhering strictly to economy regardless of other considerations. In addition to strict economy we must have an intelligent expenditure of money from one end of the country to the other along such lines as give the best promise of immediate and sure returns.
With regard to the Swift Current farm, I heard one hon. gentleman of the group to my

Supply-Experimental Farms
left complaining because the minister had established a farm at that point. I have very much pleasure indeed in exonerating the minister from all blame for that and in taking it on my own shoulders, where the responsibility rests for selecting that site. It wds chosen because it was a district just a little different from any other district where an experimental farm was situated, and I am very pleased indeed to learn that having gathered a crop or two from that land the minister has found it was a very good place to locate a farm.
In conclusion, no one has a greater appreciation of what has been done by the experimental farm system than I have. I think it is second to none in the world, as far as I have been able to gather the information, and I would be sorry indeed to see the minister do anything to radically change the most excellent work that has been carried on at these institutions. I would ask him to seriously consider before taking any such action.

I would like to say a word or two in favour of the experimental farm system. It is quite a number of years since one experiment was carried on at the Brandon farm which added much to the knowledge of what pasture grasses could do in the western country. Dr. Bedford, as he is now, when he was superintendent of the Brandon experimental farm, about the time that brome grass was being introduced, sowed one acre, fenced it with wire netting, and for the whole summer pastured two full grown steers there, showing that it only took one acre to pasture two head of cattle during the summer, whereas on the ranges in southern Alberta thirty acres is required to run one head. A lot of people visited Brandon to see that experiment, and brome grass got a start at that time that it has never lost.
I would like to back up what the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Steedsman) said in regard to the necessity for having a grass in the western country that is suitable for rotation. That is something that is absolutely needed, and if agriculture is going to be permanent in our western country, it ought to be by crop rotation. That will have to be worked out.
As regards the experiments conducted on the experimental farms, a good many people have not very much confidence in them because they figure that it is government money that is keeping up those farms. It is just a year ago last January since a resolution was passed by the convention of Agricultural Societies, sitting at the Agricultural College in Winnipeg, asking the government to commence demonstration farms, if you like to call them that. What they wanted was a farm in each locality where the average man on an, average farm could show good returns at the end of the year, raise a crop and make the farm pay. That is what is wanted, and that is one of the reasons why farmers as a rule take more stock in experiments carried on by their neighbours than by the experimental farms. First and foremost, agriculture must-be made to pay. That is what the farmer is interested in.
As regards community breeding, the minister has said that the government were absolutely behind it. Personally I think the Department of Agriculture under this government and the past government has not stood behind community breeding as I should like to see them do. Take, for instance, the federal assistance to horse breeders. There is something that I have always considered an' injustice. Federal assistance is given to a horse breeder providing that one individual owns a stallion, but in a community where a number of farmers get together and purchase a high-class sire they get no assistance whatever. I consider that wrong, and it ought to be remedied. I would be very much in favour of the government doing all it can to improve all live stock, for goodness knows it needs to be improved, and if we are going to capture the British market we will certainly have to have our cattle up to a better standard than they are in the West at the present time. Every encouragement is needed from the government. I would ask the minister to remove the injustice that exists at the present time in that no federal assistance is given to farmers trying to carry on community breeding of high-class draught horses. This does not apply to any one particular breed; all high class draught horses suffer from the same handicap.

In reply to the hon. member who has just taken his seat I may say that the question he has raised with regard to horse breeding will come up more properly under the live stock vote when I will be very pleased to discuss it very fully. I recognize that he has brought up a question that will naturally arouse a certain amount of interest among the committee.
With respect to the development of grasses, it is to the credit of the experimental farms that brome grass was introduced into western Canada. Some people think it was an evil. It is hard, of course, to eradicate, but if you can get it free from quack grass there is no substantial difficulty that cannot be surmounted in the eradication of it when once
Supply-Experimental Farms

you know how. Like everything else it is easy when you know how. It is the best grass, in my estimation, that has yet been introduced into western Canada notwithstanding the difficulty of eradication. I have grown that grass for thirty years and at one time made lots of money out of it when many people were losing money growing wheat and hauling it the distance they had to. As a matter of fact that is one way I adopted to overcome the transportation difficulty. I could haul $300 worth of grass seed to Indian Head and market it with the same team and the same handling as I could seventeen or eighteen dollars worth of wheat. That was the result of observations I made as I passed the experimental farm at Indian Head. There is no doubt about it, these farms have been of inestimable value in the past.
With respect to the complaint-the very natural complaint-made by the hon. member sitting at the back-I think the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride)-I had the pleasure of travelling with that genial companion last summer. I did hope at that time that we would be able to start one, if not two, experimental farms in that vast territory which is capable of such tremendous development. The crops there, notwithstanding the drouth which prevailed at that time, were a marvel. But, Mr. Chairman, the time has come when, even in the matter of establishing experimental farms, we must cut our coat to suit the cloth; and I would advise my hon. friend to wait a year or two until we can start that institution properly, in the meantime taking care of the older farms in the way I have described. At present there is very good work being done at Fort George, Vanderhoof, and other points with respect to illustration stations -exceedingly good work. At the same time I recognize that that will not fill the bill indefinitely. I have intimated to the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Tolmie) who had tacitly, I think, with his officials concluded to establish a farm there while he was administering the affairs of the department that I feel we are committed to that place for the location of our next new farm.
With respect to some additions to the old farms to which I have referred, I may say. that from time to time as we get the opportunity to buy five, ten, fifteen or twenty acres at a good bargain we think it is good business to do that, under the old farm system, particularly where we have to buy feed. There is scarcely a farm under the old system where we do not have to buy feed. My hon. friends opposite who have been life long farmers know
(Mr. Motherwell.]
that is not good business on their individual farms. Some times it occurs inadvertently or is unavoidable, but as a general practice it is bad. It is just as bad for the experimental farms as it is for the individual farms, and it should be avoided as far as possible in both cases. ,
Now with regard to the remarks of the hon. member for Victoria City (Mr. Tolmie), I may say that I hope I did not leave the impression that we were simply going to turn these farms upside down and convert them into exclusive breeding farms, or that we were going to revolutionize them, or that there was going to be much change in respect to many of them. But there are certain farms in the Maritime provinces and in the prairie provinces as well, where we believe we would be neglecting our duty if we did not pay- considerably more attention to live stock at this time. The farmer that insists upon continuing in exclusive farming of any kind-whether it be fruit, grain, potatoes, or any other branch-has to take his chances; he is engaged in a very much more vulnerable business economically than the man who is devoting himself to diversified farming We believe in the good old practice of diversification or specialties if you like, whatever the district may be adapted to, so that when one particular branch falls down you will have something to keep the wolf from the door, or something to prevent you from raising money on a mortgage at the bank. This doctrine is as old as the hills and a great many people are practising it.
As regards the farms to which I have referred at which more attention will be paid to live stock, I may say that at the present time Mr. Archibald has gone to the United Kingdom in connection with that work. Although we have had exceedingly good directors of the experimental farms system since their inception by Professor Wiiliam Saunders, I do not think we have had a man more active, more alive, or more energetic, than the present director, Mr. Archibald. He is about arriving in the United Kingdom on an errand in connection with certain shipments of homes. While he is there he is going to buy thirty breeding boars of the best bacon type he can find in the United Kingdom, consisting perhaps of Yorkshires, Tamworths, and a few bacon type of Berk-shires. We hope to equip our experimental farms with these, distributing them to suit the requirements of the various districts. While at the Royal fair during the early winter I was discussing this matter with some of the breeders of Tamworths, and they told

Supply-Experimental Farms
mo we could not perform a better service than by introducing some new strains of Tarn-worths. Because of the inbreeding that had been practised in this breed by the various breeders it was found that an infusion of new blood was desirable. They were delighted to find that the government contemplated bringing in shipments of this particular breed to which 1 have referred. With the demand for the bacon type of hog, and with our grading system so recently introduced, and with so few breeds grading up to standard, this is one of the activities we will undertake at the various experimental farms throughout Canada.
I may say to the hon. member for Victoria City that I went into that matter very fully and I think I satisfied the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland), so that he does not look half so savage as he did last year. If I succeeded in satisfying him I think my hon. friend from Victoria City, had he been here at the time, would have been satisfied also that we do not mean to enter upon any serious revolutionary process, nor into any field in a way calculated to disturb private enterprise, but rather to proceed in such a manner that if we act judiciously we shall encourage private enterprise. That was the extent of my argument and I think my explanations were generally accepted by the committee.

I think the minister very well stated the course that should be followed in regard to this particular item. He said we should make the suit to fit the cloth. Following up his own statement I think that he should cut off the increase of $200,000 asked for this year in connection with this vote. I want to protest very strongly against the way in which the estimates dealing with agriculture are presented to us, and I think that remark applies equally to the estimates of some of the departments. How can any man here vote intelligently to-night on the question of whether we shall spend the sum of $1,525,000 on experimental farms? I think we have spent something over three hours in discussion of the item, and I do not feel that we have had any reasonable explanation from the Minister of Agriculture as to what he is going to do with this money. I think the minister should have the items printed in detail in the estimates or at least state how much it is proposed to spend on each farm. There are a great many men in this House who do not know how many experimental farms there are in Canada, and I must admit that I am one of them. I think that we might very well put this information in the estimates. If
the minister would not consider doing that, I think we should adopt some new procedure for dealing with the estimates, so that we could deal with them intelligently.
I think they might very properly go to the Committee on Agriculture and there be discussed in detail by the members of that committee. Then I am sure when a recommendation came from that committee there would be very little opposition in this House to the passing of the estimates, and a lot of time might be saved. I for one am not prepared to vote for this large increase of expenditure in the Department of Agriculture with the explanation that we have had from the minister to-day. I do not say that he is to blame.

Will my hon. friend indicate any particular information he desires? I read out nearly all the twenty-two farms and indicated the amount we proposed to spend on each of them. I think we can supply pretty nearly any reasonable information he desires to ask for, and I will be delighted to do so.

We have spent three hours and I do not think we have yet been told the total amount it is proposed to expend, say on the experimental farm at Ottawa, or on the farm at Indian Head or on the farm at Agassiz, and just what they would do with the money at any one of these particular farms. He stated, if I understood him correctly, that the period of experimentation in regard to grain growing on the prairie was practically over for these farms, and yet he asks for an increased vote of $200,000. To my mind he certainly is not justified in asking for that increase without any explanation. He says that he proposes to expend $5,000 on one farm and $3,000 on another but gave no real substantial reason for what is being done. I think the experimental farm is a necessity in Canada. There is one necessary work that the farm should perform, and that is research work, with regard to plant diseases and insect pests and such things. Those are matters that the average farmer cannot handle. In western Canada a great deal of the best experimental work has been done by individual farmers and not by experimental farms. I am not for a minute running down the work done on our experimental farms. Good work has been done on these farms but much of it has not been made use of by the individual fanner. We are trying to bring the individual farmer to the experimental farm, instead of taking the experimental farm to the individual farmer and it is a very hard thing to do. I think a lot of our money might be far better spent in employing agricultural agents to

travel round and visit the farms. I think the Minister of Agriculture might close up the Rosthern farm. He says it is going to be moved, and yet he is going to spend this year several thousand dollars more than was spent last year.
I do not want to weary the House with any more remarks, but I really have not been convinced that we are wise in voting the extra $200,000 for the experimental farms this year.

My hon. friend has made two or three suggestions that look good on the face of them, and are good, except that they do not come properly under this vote. The question of insect pests comes under the very next vote, and when we reach it we will deal with the part the experimental farms throughout the Dominion play in regard to this important question. That is a question rapidly growing in importance, but I do not think it advisable to mix up with this matter.
With respect to the agricultural agents, I say; yes, employ them, if you can get the right kind of men, but that is an up-to-date provincial matter. While that is so, the grant the Dominion has been giving for the last ten years under the Agricultural Instruction Acts has been devoted largely in the direction of paying the district representatives in the various provinces. In Ontario I do not know what percentage of the district representatives are paid out of the Dominion grant, but it is a very substantial number. So that if you take the questions in the consecutive order in which they appear in the estimates, you will find all that work will be covered before we are through. Furthermore, with respect to the meagre information outlined in the estimates, I must confess myself, Mr. Chairman, that when I saw the amount that was published last year as compared with provincial estimates with which I had been familiar, it did not look excessive, but I am accepting these matters just as I find them. This is the second estimate that I have had the responsibility of explaining, and my hon. friend's suggestion that more details might be given in connection with this vote is, I think, deserving of some consideration. I think my hon. friend will at least admit that just to the extent that this is lacking, I have endeavoured not to be lacking in explaining the votes for the various activities that we have undertaken in this department, I have been trying to avoid the very thing my hon. friend complains of-spending too much time. I took about three-quarters of an hour at the outset trying to give a bird's eye view, a

sort of skeleton, of the work, so that the committee might have a very intelligent grasp of the whole situation as to what was our objective and our plans with respect to the future in regard to new farms and all that sort of thing. I do not know whether that saved any time or not, but I do hope it gave members who are not intimately associated with, or who do not live in close proximity to the farms, some idea of the matter. The suggestion that we should give more particulars is a matter of general policy that might be taken up by the government, not only with regard to these estimates, but possibly all others.

The hon. gentleman who
spoke a few minutes ago asked for particular information. The hon. minister (Mr. Motherwell) took five minutes in giving us a resume, but that does not give us the information we wanted. The question asked by the hon. gentleman from Macleod (Mr. Coote) was how much money was spent on the Central Experimental farm last year and how much it is proposed to spend on that farm this year. These are questions I would like to see answered.

I went over that
once already.

to get it.

The increase, I think, was $5,000. Therefore, by deducting $5,000 from $44,550, you will get what was spent last year, or, in round figures, $39,550.
What is the figure for Ros-thern?

The minister, in giving us the estimated expenditure for the Central farm for this year, said that it included some other experimental stations. Can he not tell us the expenditures in connection with those experimental stations, so that we can arrive at a positive idea of the cost of the central farm for this year?

It is pretty hard to state exactly the cost of the Central Experimental farm, because that is really the clearing house for the entire twenty-two branch farm system. Experiments in regard to grasses, grains, etc., are conducted there, and as soon as it is established that they are of sufficient importance to develop, they are sent to the various farms and planted there in what we call multiplier plots, where they are developed. Therefore, more or less of the work of the Central Experimental farm is really chargeable to the branch farms, because of this dovetailing. It is one entire layout, as it were. If my hon. friend wants any particular division of the Central Experimental farm system-

No, I want to know what the central farm is costing, and I think that
is a fair question. If the minister says that those smaller farms throughout the country cost certain sums and those certain sums all added together constitute the total cost of them, the balance must be the expenditure for the central farm. Surely, we should be able to arrive at a figure showing the cost of the central farm. The matter is only one of bookkeeping.

The minister, in his remarks a few moments ago, seemed to insinuate that we might have asked for this information earlier. It is true, we might have asked for it earlier, and if I had had an opportunity I would have asked for it myself. But a number of members were asking questions and I did not have' an opportunity. There are only some twenty-two experimental farms, and the minister should give us a list of them and the expenditures in connection with each. I have expressed my views on this question in the past, and I repeat to-night that this is altogether too large an expenditure for the work that is done on this farm. In the face of that you are not able to demonstrate to the people on any farm adjacent to the Central Experimental farm what the cost of farming is. You cannot show that the people are or are not justified in their complaints with regard to the condition of agriculture. Notwithstanding the fact that for ordinary farm labour you are spending no less than $182,365 at the Central Experimental farm, you are unable to show what is the actual cost of farm operations. The item under discussion has a bearing on an item further down, namely, the decrease in the Health of Animals branch. I think it can be readily shown that experimental farms are well worth all the money that is expended on them. To realize this -we have only to remember the provincial experimental farm at Guelph and the introduction there of Mandecheuria barley by Dr. Zavitz, which it is estimated has already benefited our farmers to the extent of 830,000,000. The introduction of Marquis wheat has been referred to this evening, and I suppose that has meant hundreds of millions of dollars in the pockets of the farmers of Canada. Only recently we noticed in the newspapers an announcement of the discovery of another variety of wheat, Marquis III, which is expected to play a very important part in our agriculture. Now, hon. members, will understand that in experimental farm work where the grain has to be set out in little plots, much of it has to be hand picked, and great care taken to keep it separate from other grains, that the work is costly, and that
viewed from that restricted standpoint an experimental farm cannot be made to show a profit; but viewed generally by the results to the people of Canada, why, such a farm pays about as well as anything with which Canada has to do. For that reason I should like very much to support this increase of $200,000, but when I find that we have a decrease of $285,000 suggested in the Health of Animals branch, I find myself unable to endorse the former. What is the use of spending $200,000 to introduce better live stock if we neglect the health of animals? As the minister said to-night, they have been standing pat at these experimental farms for eight years, and they can stand pat for another year in regard to the introduction of live stock and get along all right with what they have already; but we cannot stand pat when it comes to a question of disease or health. If we neglect the health of a human being or an animal for a single year, we cannot mark time, we are bound to go back. Nov/, this country has established a system which has held in check to some extent the plague of tuberculosis, and last year more than ever before in our cities waged a very active campaign in the same direction. But notwithstanding the progress made we find that this important work is to all go by the board. As I say, I should like to see this increase go through. I believe it is a good investment for Canada, but if it is to be at the sacrifice of the other item I have referred to, I cannot support it.

Mr. Chairman, this is going to entail a discussion of another vote altogether, but I think it should be permitted because the hon. gentleman's remarks are reasonable enough, unless I can show a valid explanation for the reduction. Our intention is to take care of that work for another year just as effectually as we did last year.

If I may be permitted to interrupt the minister? When I was down at the office where this work is conducted I was informed that if this vote goes through as reduced there will be no new work carried on this year.

If you will permit this digression, Mr. Chairman, I shall be very pleased to enter into the question, for the hon. member for Portage la Prairie appears to be quite exercised over it.
Not at all.

I suppose my hon. friends are aware of the fact that there is what is called follow-up work in regard to accredited herds, that you have to give a second examination, that that examination invariably finds very much fewer reactors than the first examination; but if we are to keep the accredited herds clean there must be a second examination given in a reasonable time. That is what we are engaged on now. That will keep our staff busy, at very much less expense, and enable us to get through this current year reasonably well. We are not taking on any new accredited herds. We had to do the same thing last year. What we are doing now is to take care of the herds already accredited, and unless you engage in that follow-up work your original work is of no value in a very few years. I may say for the benefit of my hon. friends that I-lost an entire herd through tuberculosis before there was any compensation, so I know exactly what the loss means to the individual. But the compensation to-day is so high that it frustrates the very object it has in view. A compensation of S200 for many animals that I know of will buy the animals, and the man who gets that figure or two-thirds of it will be getting a much better figure than he would on the market to-day in a lot of cases. *The original framers of this scheme of compensation never had the idea in mind of giving more compensation than the animal was worth.
Are not the animals valued by the officials of the department at their actual worth?
I know they are, but the maximum valuation is $200, and two-thirds of that is $133, and I know plenty of animals that are not worth that.

Is not the minister misinterpreting the act? I am no specialist on this, but as I understand the minister's own explanation, it is this:	The animal is valued
but no valuation is allowed beyond $200, and though the animal may be valued by his own officers at $200, there cannot be paid more than two-thirds of that. The owner is never paid more than two-thirds of the value fixed by the minister's own officers. How does he

rqake that consistent with the assertion that more money is paid than the animal is worth?
So it is; $133 is more than many of them are worth.

That is the maximum
value. There is nothing to prevent a man from valuing them down as low as he likes. If this subject is open for discussion-I do not want to be out of order-

I am perfectly satisfied to bow to your ruling.

Might I say, Mr. Chairman, that in what is called a restricted area in Manitoba we are cleaning up tuberculosis in all animals regardless of whether they are grade or pure-bred. That is costing some $75,000, and we are doing it as a try-out for the purpose of finding out what it is going to cost. That will not be required in next year's vote, and accounts for $75,000. The second examination, which will take up the time of the staff but will not require nearly so much money, will account for a little more, and I hope that the reduction that will be provided with respect to compensation for certain animals will account for some more. So we shall be able to carry on the work just as effectively as last year.
The reason we are trying out this restricted area of three municipalities in Manitoba is this, and I am sure my predecessor understands the situation:	If this work is
going to run into a large sum of money we want to be able to go to the provinces and to the municipalities and ask for their cooperation in cleaning up the herds regardless of whether they are grade or pure bred. In the United States they have adopted a plan whereby the federal government, state legislatures and municipalities unite in this work. We hope to get some information from the work in this restricted area that we can place before the provinces and the municipalities, and possibly at some conference suggest to them, are you prepared to enter into cooperation with the federal authorities with a view to taking care of this very heavy and very necessary and important work? That is the method adopted in the United States, and it has been found to work out effectively. I do not know whether it will work out effectively here, but I must have the information as to the cost before I can hope to have the

Supply-Experimental Farms
co-operation of the provinces and municipalities. That sum will not be required next year and that accounts for a very large portion of that reduction.

Is it not a fact that the maximum valuation of an animal is $200, that only two-thirds of that is paid, and that it is strictly the duty of the official carrying out that work to fix the actual market value of the animal before entering up his compensation papers? That actual market value might be only twenty or thirty or fifty dollars, and you are only entitled by law to pay two-thirds of that amount. I am sure the minister would not want the statement to go abroad that his officials were fixing these papers or preparing false papers. I have known the men doing this work in the Health of Animals branch for many years, and they are gentlemen of repute and high standing in their profession, and I would hate to see the statement go out imputing wrong statements to these men in the preparation of their papers.

My hon. friend knows perfectly well the difficulty. If you put the compensation high, you are going to have the valuation high; there is no question about that. This is one of the most difficult features of our whole compensation business, to get a proper valuation that will compensate the owner partially. It is similar to the indemnity that is paid to members; it is an indemnity, not a salary, and similarly the compensation is paid to the man to indemnify him for his loss, so that with the salvage of the animal and the compensation, he can start over again. It may be sound theoretically to say that if we put the compensation up to $1,000 the appraisers would value the animals at their actual value, but would not the tendency be to appraise the animal higher than if the maximum compensation was $200? There is no question in my mind that that would be the tendency. That has been my experience, and it is no reflection on the staff at all. If we are going to have a successful administration of this Vote we shall have to give reasonable satisfaction and secure the active and sympathetic co-operation of the owners of the stock. The desire of the breeders to have their herds accredited goes to show that they are being well compensated for their stock now. I do not believe that the intention of the framers of the act is being carried out if no part of the loss falls on the owner of the animal. It is true that a lot of the loss falls on breeders of first-class
stock, but with regard to inferior animals the present compensation means that you are buying the animal.

I have had a number of years' experience in the actual administration of the act, first as inspector in the employ of the federal government, and also as chief inspector for the province of British Columbia, and I say that if you are paying more money than these cattle are worth to-day the act is not being carried out, and anybody that does that should be fired immediately.
In the first place an inspector makes his valuation in the field. That valuation certificate is submitted to the chief inspector of the province, who looks over it carefully, and if he requires more information secures it from the inspector in the field. Finally those documents are forwarded to the head office in Ottawa, where they are submitted to further scrutiny. There is no man who is doing his duty who will value the animal higher than its actual worth. It is his business to base the valuation on the regular market price, and if he wishes further information on this particular subject he can easily obtain it by applying to those who keep in close touch with the market reports. As I said before, anybody valuing these animals at a greater value than they are worth on the market is certainly not fulfilling his duties and should be looked after and reprimanded.
Then, it does not make any difference what the maximum valuation is, whether it is $200 or $2,000. The appraiser will come along and give the real value.

A few days ago I had occasion to read in the House a paragraph from a journal making certain allegations. That excerpt is already on Hansard and it it not necessary to repeat it. It was stated that this practice was carried on on quite a large scale around the stockyards at Winnipeg.

I absolutely do not believe that statement for one minute. I know these men in the Health of Animals branch. I know their reputation and I know they are
